CLASS 34 · AGES 4–5 · 29 WEATHER LESSONS

Weather, Seasons & What We Wear.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Read the sky, then dress for it.

Every topic in this class has its own step-by-step lesson: look at the picture together, learn what the weather or the garment really is, say the parent script, ask the questions, play the practice game and finish with a small understanding check. The order is gentle: the sun and clouds first, then the weather words, then the day-kinds — sunny, rainy, stormy, snowy, foggy — then the temperatures, the four seasons, and finally the clothes that match every kind of sky.

The best part of this class is that the weather marks your homework. After the sunny-day lesson, a sunny day arrives for free practice; after the raincoat lesson, so does the rain. One topic a day is plenty — the whole class is a month of five-minute sessions, wherever your child’s curiosity points.

WEATHER SAFETY, AGE-HONEST

Small people, real weather.

Weather safety is built into the lessons where it belongs: never staring at the sun, hats and water in the heat, staying inside for storms, penguin steps on ice, bright colours in fog, scarf ends tucked in for climbing. Every rule is phrased for four-year-old bodies and honest about feelings — no scare tactics, no fake promises, just routines that hold.

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Sun — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what the sun actually does for us — light, warmth, growth and shadows — and builds the sun-respect habits that keep eyes and skin happy all summer.

What is this?

The sun is the star that lights our daytime and warms our world. It rises, crosses the sky and sets, and everything on Earth — plants, animals, people — arranges its day around its light.

What does it mean?

Sunlight does three big jobs at child height: it lets us see, it warms the ground and the air, and it feeds the plants that become our food. Where sunlight falls, shadows form on the other side — the sun is always the reason for a shadow.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three suns: the friendly sun that warms and lights; the bright sun that must never be stared at because its light is too strong for our eyes; and the summer sun whose heat asks for a hat, water and shade.

Why this matters

The sun is a child’s first astronomy and first safety lesson in one object. Pointing at the sun, tracking its shadows and feeling its warmth build real scientific reasoning — and respecting its brightness is a habit that protects eyesight for life.

What it teaches

Cause-and-effect thinking (sun out, shadows sharp), temperature vocabulary, time concepts through the sun’s daily journey, observation skills, and early self-care: hat, water and shade become the child’s own decisions.

Words to learn

sunsunshineshadowwarmbrightsunrisesunsetshade

Say this to your child

“"The sun gives us light so our eyes can see and warmth so we are cosy. It helps the flowers grow tall. We love the sun from far away — we never stare at it, and on hot sunny days we wear our hats and drink water."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the sun. It gives us light to see and warmth to feel."
  2. Read the picture together: the guide points up at the sun in the sky, wears sunglasses, puts on a sun hat, rests under a tree and holds a thermometer that reads 30 degrees.
  3. Do the two-spot test: stand one moment in sunshine, one in shade. Which feels warmer? That warm feeling IS the sun.
  4. Teach the eye rule with respect, not fright: the sun is too bright to look at straight on — we admire it the way we admire a lamp, from the side, never staring.
  5. Finish with the sunny-day plan: hat on, water bottle filled, play in the shade when the sun is strongest. Act all three out right now.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a guide in a straw hat stands in a sunny park: he points toward the sun high in the blue sky, holds his hand out to notice the bright light, puts on dark sunglasses, places his hat on his head, sits resting in the shade of a big tree, and holds a white thermometer that reads 30°C. Every panel is a real sunny-day action your child can copy.

Ask your child

"What does the sun give us?" "Where does a shadow come from?" "Which spot feels warmer — the sunshine or the shade?" "What do we never do with our eyes at the sun?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The sun warms my face," "My shadow follows me because the sun is up," or the safety line: "I never look right at the sun — it is too bright."

Out in the real world

Chase shadows on the walk to preschool — long in the morning, stubby at midday, long again in the evening. Notice sun-warmed surfaces: the bench that bakes, the car door that glows, the sand at the park that heats through your shoes.

Try it together

Shadow tag in the garden: step on each other’s shadows instead of bodies. Then shadow freeze — when the sun "hides" behind a cloud, everyone freezes; when it peeks out, shadows dance again. Finish with a chalk line around a shadow and re-check it after lunch: it moved!

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the sun give us? Where must we never look? What do we wear on a hot sunny day?" Light-plus-warmth, never-stare, hat-and-water — three hits and the lesson has landed.

Parent tips

Model the eye rule yourself — if you squint and turn away from the sun, narrate it: "Too bright for my eyes, I will look down here." Children copy what you do with your face far faster than what you say. And keep hats by the door so grabbing one is automatic.

Staying safe

Never look directly at the sun — not with eyes alone, not through sunglasses as a "test". On hot days: hat, water breaks and shade rests, sunscreen applied by a grown-up, and never wait inside a parked car, not even for a minute.

This lesson pairs with the Sun flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Clouds — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns "what are clouds?" from a shrug into a skill: your child learns what clouds hold, how to tell a fine-day cloud from a rain cloud, and how to watch the sky like a little forecaster.

What is this?

Clouds are collections of tiny water drops floating high in the air — so light they drift, so many they shade whole cities. They are not smoke or candyfloss; they are water you can see from far away.

What does it mean?

Every cloud is a weather flag. White, fluffy clouds usually travel with a fine day. Grey, heavy-looking clouds are carrying more water — often rain on the way. Watching clouds move and change is reading the sky’s own news.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three cloud ideas: clouds are made of tiny water drops; white puffy clouds usually mean a nice day while grey heavy ones hint at rain; and clouds drift and change shape because the wind pushes them along.

Why this matters

Clouds are the perfect first forecast tool — visible, free, changing daily. Reading them builds comparison vocabulary (light/dark, big/small, high/low) and the scientist’s habit of gathering clues before announcing a conclusion.

What it teaches

Observation and comparison, early prediction ("grey cloud, maybe rain"), shape-naming and imagination through cloud figures, weather vocabulary, and patient watching — a full minute of quiet sky-watching is a real attention win at this age.

Words to learn

cloudfluffygreydrizzlefloatskywindrain cloud

Say this to your child

“"Clouds are tiny drops of water floating high in the sky. White fluffy clouds usually mean a lovely day. When the clouds turn grey and heavy, they might be full of rain. We can read the clouds like a book!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Clouds are made of lots and lots of tiny drops of water, floating high above us."
  2. Read the picture: the meteorologist looks at cloud shapes through a magnifying glass, watches clouds move, compares light clouds with dark clouds on a chart, checks a weather vane, draws a cloud and reads the forecast on a screen.
  3. Do the light-versus-dark test on the real sky today: find a white cloud and a grey cloud. Which one might be carrying rain?
  4. Watch one cloud move for a slow count of ten — it shifts. Something invisible is pushing it: the wind.
  5. Start a cloud diary: each morning, one quick drawing of today’s clouds. After a week, look back and find the rainiest-looking page.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a meteorologist in a white lab coat works beside a big window: she studies cloud shapes through a magnifying glass beside a cloud-types poster, looks through binoculars, points at a chart comparing light clouds with dark clouds, holds a weather vane, sketches a cloud in a notepad and points at a forecast screen showing three days — partly sunny, cloudy, rainy.

Ask your child

"What are clouds made of?" "Which cloud looks like it carries rain?" "Can you see the clouds moving?" "What shape does that cloud look like to you?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Clouds are tiny drops of water," "That grey cloud might drop rain!" or proudly report a cloud shape: "That one is a dinosaur — now it is a boat!"

Out in the real world

Check the sky before dressing each morning and let the clouds help pick the coat. At the bus stop, find the fastest-moving cloud. Airport days and tall buildings give cloud-level views that make the floating obvious.

Try it together

Cloud charades: lie back and take turns "being" a cloud shape for the other to guess. Then the rain-cloud game — start as a small white puff, grow bigger and greyer as your child piles on cushions, and end with a gentle finger-rain drizzle all over the carpet.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are clouds made of? Which clouds might bring rain? What pushes the clouds along?" Drops, the grey ones, the wind — three answers, one little forecaster born.

Parent tips

Resist the urge to make cloud-watching a quiz — the magic is in the lying-back and the noticing. If your child invents cloud animals, join in happily; imagination is the doorway through which observation walks. Keep the diary drawings tiny — ten seconds each.

Staying safe

Pick cloud-watching spots away from roads and water. On bright days, shade or a hat first — nobody should squint upward into glare. And if the sky turns properly dark and rumbling, that is a cloud lesson for another day: inside we go.

This lesson pairs with the Clouds flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Rain — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson explains where rain actually comes from and what it does for the world, then turns the next shower into a science station — drops to feel, rain to hear and a jar that measures the sky.

What is this?

Rain is water falling from the clouds. Water in seas, rivers and puddles rises up as invisible vapour, gathers into clouds, and when the drops grow big and heavy — down they come as rain.

What does it mean?

Rain is the world’s watering can. It drinks the gardens, fills the rivers and reservoirs, washes the air and the leaves, and tops up every puddle. Every drop is on a loop: ground to cloud to ground again, over and over.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three rain ideas: rain comes from water held in clouds; rain gives every plant and animal the water they need; and rainy days ask for rain gear — and offer puddles.

Why this matters

Rain is the entry point to the water cycle, the science story your child will retell for years. It also carries emotional weather: some children find rain gloomy, some find it cosy. Welcoming both feelings teaches that all weather — and all moods — passes.

What it teaches

Circular cause-and-effect (the water loop), sensory vocabulary for sound and touch, care for living things (the garden drinks too), patient measuring, and the dressing-sequencing skills that rainy mornings demand.

Words to learn

rainraindroppuddlesplashsoakshowerumbrellawellies

Say this to your child

“"Rain is how the clouds water the whole world — the trees, the flowers, you and me. Water goes up to make clouds, then falls back down as rain, then goes up again. On rainy days we wear our raincoat and boots, and the puddles are waiting."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Rain is water falling from the clouds — the clouds are giving the world a drink."
  2. Read the picture: the girl feels raindrops land on her hand, listens to the rain with her eyes closed, collects rainwater in a big blue barrel from a pipe, wears a yellow raincoat, points at a puddle and checks a forecast that reads 18 degrees.
  3. Trace the water loop with your finger in the air: puddle → up to the cloud → rain → puddle again. It never ends!
  4. Catch the next rain on the doorstep: feel a drop on a palm, listen to it on the hood, watch it bead and run off the raincoat — the coat works!
  5. Put a jar outside before bed and measure the catch in the morning: that much sky-water fell while you slept.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a girl in a green hat and green overalls stands in a rainy garden: she holds her palm out to feel the raindrops, cups her ear to listen with eyes closed, watches rainwater pour from a big pipe into a blue barrel, wears a yellow hooded raincoat, crouches to point at a puddle and holds a tablet showing a rain-cloud forecast at 18°C.

Ask your child

"Where does rain come from?" "Who drinks the rain?" "What do we put on before a rainy walk?" "What happens to puddles when the sun comes back?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Rain comes from the clouds," "The garden is drinking!" or the dressing report: "Raincoat zipped, hood up, boots on — ready!"

Out in the real world

Watch rain land in the birdbath, the sandpit cover and the watering can. Visit a rain barrel at a community garden. Notice which things love rain (worms, washed cars, ducks) and which hide from it (cats, picnics, chalk drawings).

Try it together

Puddle symphony: tap a tray of water slowly, then fast, then drum the rim — which sounds like today’s rain? Then the water-loop pantomime: everyone crouches as a "puddle", rises as vapour, huddles as a cloud, and sprinkle-falls back down as rain.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does rain come from? What does rain give the garden? What do we wear in the rain?" Clouds, a drink, raincoat-and-boots — the loop is learned.

Parent tips

Do not rush to comfort a child who grumbles at rain — hand them the measuring jar or the listening game instead, and let the rain become interesting before it becomes background. And own the gear: a child who picked their own wellies begs for rain.

Staying safe

Rain makes slopes, painted lines and leaves slippery — walking feet near roads, always. Wet roads make cars slower to stop, so hands are held at crossings. And when thunder joins the rain, the lesson shifts to storm rules: inside, cosy, away from windows.

This lesson pairs with the Rain flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Rainbow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson explains the rainbow’s two ingredients — sunshine and raindrops — walks the seven colours in order, and gives your family the mist-spray trick that puts a rainbow in your own hands.

What is this?

A rainbow is a giant arc of coloured light. It appears when the sun shines through falling raindrops: each drop splits the white light into its colours, and together the drops paint the arc across the sky.

What does it mean?

A rainbow needs both of its ingredients at once: light from behind you, rain in front of you. That is why rainbows visit right after showers and fade when the drops dry. The colours always arrive in the same order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three rainbow ideas: rainbows come from sun plus rain; the colours follow a fixed seven-colour order; and rainbows are quick visitors — enjoy them now, draw them later.

Why this matters

A rainbow bundles colour knowledge, sequencing and the first optics into one unforgettable sight. Naming seven colours in order is genuine memorisation practice — and the brief visit teaches, gently, that some wonderful things do not last, which is a big feeling made safe.

What it teaches

Colour naming and ordering, sequential memory, light-and-water science, the emotional literacy of enjoying-and-letting-go, and art transfer — drawing the rainbow afterwards keeps both the colours and the memory.

Words to learn

rainbowarccolourslightraindropsprismfadesky

Say this to your child

“"A rainbow comes when sun and rain are both in the sky. The sunbeam dives into the raindrops and comes out in seven colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Rainbows do not stay long — we enjoy them, then we draw them so they stay with us."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "When the sun shines through raindrops, the light splits into its colours — a rainbow!"
  2. Read the picture: the scientist spots a rainbow over a house, crouches by a puddle with a special glass that splits light, points at a chart naming all seven colours, shades her eyes from the sun, draws a rainbow with crayons and stands between two thought bubbles — a rain cloud and a smiling sun.
  3. Chant the seven colours with finger-counts: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Again, faster. Again, whispering.
  4. Teach the recipe like a cake: sunshine behind you + raindrops ahead = rainbow. Both, same time, that is the whole trick.
  5. Try the kitchen version on a sunny day: fine water mist from a hose or spray bottle, sun behind you — hunt the little rainbow hiding in the spray.

Look closer at the picture

The rainbow card follows a scientist with round glasses and a white lab coat: she points up at a big rainbow arcing over a house and trees, kneels by a puddle holding a special glass that bends light, presents a whiteboard with seven labelled colour dots — Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet — shades her eyes from a bright sun, colours a rainbow band picture with crayons, and gestures between a rain-cloud bubble and a smiling-sun bubble as if explaining how both make it together.

Ask your child

"What two things make a rainbow?" "Which colour comes first? Which is last?" "Why do rainbows go away?" "What could we do to keep the memory?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might chant the seven colours unprompted for days, announce "Sun plus rain makes rainbow!" from the back seat of the car, or declare the mist-spray rainbow the best discovery of the summer.

Out in the real world

Keep rainbow-spotting alive all season: after every shower, check the sky in the shower’s direction with the sun at your back. Garden sprinklers, car washes and fountain spray all hide little rainbows on sunny days.

Try it together

Rainbow restaurant: lay out coloured paper "plates" and serve toy food sorted to each colour band. Rainbow hunt at home: find one object per colour, laid on the floor in arc order. Then the big art: a seven-band crayon rainbow, one colour chanted per band.

Understanding check

Ask: "What makes a rainbow? Name the colours you remember. Why can we not keep a rainbow?" Sun-plus-rain, any ordered run of the seven, and a soft "it fades" — that is the full arc.

Parent tips

When a real rainbow fades mid-hug, let the disappointment exist and answer it with action: "Let us draw it quick, before we forget!" The drawing ritual converts loss into making. And learn the colours yourself by heart — confidence is contagious.

Staying safe

Rainbow-hunting means back to the sun — say it out loud together: we look at the rainbow sky, never at the sun. Wet grass and slopes are slippery, so rainbow-chasing feet walk. Spray-bottle rainbows are for sunny days, never for eyes.

This lesson pairs with the Rainbow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Wind — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes invisible air visible: your child learns what wind is, gathers the clues that show it blowing, and ends with the season’s best prize — flying a kite safely in an open field.

What is this?

Wind is air that is moving. Air is everywhere around us, and when a lot of it travels in one direction we feel it as a breeze on our cheeks, hear it in the trees and see it in everything it pushes.

What does it mean?

Wind has jobs and moods. Gentle wind dries washing, cools hot picnics, carries seeds and spins the big turbines that make electricity. Strong wind bends trees, waves washing on the line and chases hats down the street.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three wind ideas: wind is moving air we feel but never see; we know wind is blowing because of what it moves — leaves, branches, washing, wind socks; and windy days ask for hat-holding, and give kite-flying.

Why this matters

Wind is the purest inference lesson in early science: the cause is invisible, so the child reasons entirely from effects. That clue-gathering — leaves moving, sock pointing, hair flying — is the exact thinking scientists use to study things too big or small to see.

What it teaches

Inference from evidence, gradient words (breeze, gust, gale), cause-and-effect through kite flying, gross-motor play against resistance, and safety judgement about flying objects and open spaces.

Words to learn

windbreezegustblowwind sockkitefluttergusty

Say this to your child

“"Wind is air on the move. We cannot see it, but we can see what it does: the leaves dance, the washing flaps, the wind sock stretches out. On windy days we hold our hats — and on a good steady windy day, we fly a kite!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Wind is air that is moving — we cannot see air, but we can see what it does!"
  2. Read the picture: the engineer in a white hard hat and high-visibility vest feels the breeze on her hand, watches a red-and-white wind sock stretch out, sees leaves blown off a tree, holds her hat on her head, flies a red-and-yellow kite and points at a tablet that says WINDY. Behind her: giant white wind turbines.
  3. Collect wind clues right now: hold a hand out the door — feel it? Throw a scrap of tissue — watch it fly. Which way is the wind pointing today?
  4. Sort the moods: a breeze tickles, a gust pushes, a gale grabs hats. Act all three with your hands and voices.
  5. Book the kite: windy day + open field + grown-up = kite day. Practise the run-and-release at home first with a ribbon on a stick.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a wind-farm engineer wears a white hard hat, a navy shirt and a yellow high-visibility vest with a wind-turbine badge: she feels the wind on her raised palm, stands beside a striped wind sock on a pole, watches green leaves blow from a branch, steadies her hard hat with both hands, flies a red-and-yellow diamond kite with bows on its tail, and shows a tablet with wind icons and the word WINDY. Tall white turbines turn in the background.

Ask your child

"What is wind made of?" "How do we know the wind is blowing if we cannot see it?" "What does the wind do to our hats?" "Where do kites fly best?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The wind is pushing the leaves!" "A breeze is small and a gale is HUGE," or the field report: "My kite flew because the wind pulled it up."

Out in the real world

Count wind workers on any street: washing lines, flags, wind turbines on hills, the trees leaning after a storm. Weather-vane visits, harbour sails and windy-day bus stops all show the air doing visible work.

Try it together

Wind orchestra: paper strips, balloons and a fan — which things does the fan move, which ignore it? Then streamer racing: whose streamer flies straightest? Finish with the classic — faces into the breeze, eyes closed, one deep breath: you just felt the whole sky move.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is wind? Name two things the wind moves. What do we hold on a windy day?" Moving air, any two honest movers, and hats — the invisible is now visible.

Parent tips

Answer "what makes wind?" simply and honestly: air moves from place to place, like a crowd shuffling — warm air rises, cool air slides in, and that shuffle is wind. No need for pressure maps at four; the shuffle picture is enough and it is true.

Staying safe

Skip tree-lined streets and building sites on gusty days — branches and debris travel. Kites fly in open fields far from roads and power lines, launch and landing by a grown-up. And secure or leave home anything the wind can turn into a projectile: hats, balloons, lightweight toys.

This lesson pairs with the Wind flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Snow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson explains what snow actually is — frozen water falling in tiny crystals — and turns the first snowfall into a full science morning: catch, measure, melt, then warm up properly.

What is this?

Snow is water that froze into tiny ice crystals high in the clouds and fell as soft white flakes. Each flake is a little six-sided star of ice, and each one melts back into a drop of water when it lands on something warm.

What does it mean?

Snow needs cold all the way down — the whole air column must be chilly or the flakes arrive as rain or sleet. Fresh snow covers the ground in a white blanket, muffles sounds, records every footprint and melts back into water that feeds the spring.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three snow ideas: snow is frozen water in crystal flakes; flakes melt on warm hands because our bodies are warm; and snow play asks for the full warm kit — coat, hat, gloves and boots — with warm-up breaks inside.

Why this matters

Snow is the most touchable science in childhood: children hold crystals, watch them vanish, pack them, stack them and measure them. Melting is their first change-of-state experiment, and the ruler in the snow is their first measuring instrument used for a real question.

What it teaches

Change-of-state understanding (ice ⇄ water), measurement skills with real stakes, cold-body awareness and self-advocacy ("my gloves are wet"), shape observation on sleeves, and the sequencing of a full dressing routine.

Words to learn

snowsnowflakemeltfreezeicefrostsnowballslippery

Say this to your child

“"Snow is frozen water falling in tiny star-shaped flakes. Catch one on your sleeve and look quick — then watch it melt on your hand, because our hands are warm. In the snow we wear all our warm kit and walk like penguins on the slippery bits."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Snow is rain that froze into tiny ice stars on the way down."
  2. Read the picture: the girl in a blue pom-pom hat catches a falling snowflake on her hand, kneels to measure the snow with a big ruler, fastens her warm coat, rolls a snowball, walks carefully on an icy path and reads a forecast that says Snow, minus 2 degrees.
  3. Teach the melt: catch one flake on a dark sleeve and watch it closely; then one on a warm palm — gone! Our hands are warm enough to turn snow back into water.
  4. Measure together: stand a ruler in the snow, read the number, check again after an hour. Snow grows and shrinks — like a science pet.
  5. Drill the kit in order: coat, hat, gloves, boots — then the penguin walk on icy paths, tiny steps, knees soft.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a girl in a blue pom-pom beanie with a snowflake pattern and a blue winter jacket: holds her hand out to catch one big six-pointed snowflake, kneels beside a numbered ruler standing in the snow to measure its depth, zips her coat up to her chin, rolls a big round snowball, walks with careful steps along a snowy path between fences and snowy pines, and points at a tablet reading "Snow −2°C" with little flakes on the screen.

Ask your child

"What is snow made of?" "Why did the flake melt on your hand?" "How deep is the snow on our ruler?" "What do we wear before snow play?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Snowflakes are little ice stars!" "It melted because my hand is warm," or the kit chant: "Coat, hat, gloves, boots — ready for snow!"

Out in the real world

Watch snow line rooftops, hide the grass and outline every branch after a night of steady fall. Find where snow melts first (sunny edges, warm car roofs) and where it lingers (shady corners). Track a snowman through its slow, sagging goodbye.

Try it together

Snow-kitchen: bowls, spoons and cupcake trays turn fresh snow into the year’s best sensory table. Melt-race: one cup of snow indoors, one outside — which melts faster, and why? Then the snowball school: pack, roll, stop — and the family rule about where snowballs may never fly.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is snow? Why do flakes melt in your hand? Name your snow-day kit." Frozen water, warm hands, and any full run of coat-hat-gloves-boots — the lesson has landed.

Parent tips

Keep spare gloves drying by the radiator — the wet-glove swap keeps the outing alive twice as long. And capture the melting question every time: "Where did the snow go?" is a genuine science prompt, and "it turned to water!" is a genuinely correct answer.

Staying safe

Wet plus cold chills bodies fast — full kit with waterproof boots, and dry gloves the moment they soak through. Penguin steps on icy paths, never eat snow, snowballs never at faces or cars, and inside when shivers start. Snow that has been played in is for playing, not for tasting.

This lesson pairs with the Snow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Weather Forecast — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns the morning forecast into a family ritual: what forecasts are, who makes them, how to read the little icons, and how the sky’s plan decides the coat, the hat and the day.

What is this?

A weather forecast is a careful prediction of what the sky will do next — today, tomorrow, all week. Weather scientists read maps, clouds and instruments, then share the plan on TV, radio and phones.

What does it mean?

Forecasts turn unknown skies into known plans: rain icon means the wellies come out, sun icon means the sun hat, storm warning means the family stays close to home. The forecast does not control the sky — it just reads the clues early.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three forecast ideas: the forecast tells us what the sky plans before it happens; sun, cloud and rain icons are the forecast’s picture words; and families use the forecast to choose clothes and to stay safe when big weather comes.

Why this matters

Checking the forecast is daily evidence-based decision-making in child-size form: information → choice → action → check the result. Children adore grading the forecaster’s homework — and grading an adult’s work respectfully is a genuine critical-thinking exercise.

What it teaches

Prediction and verification, icon literacy, planning and sequencing (what comes first — coat or boots?), weather vocabulary across days (today, tomorrow, the whole week), and the family-habit feeling that preparation beats surprise.

Words to learn

forecastpredictweather reporterplanicontomorrowweeklystorm warning

Say this to your child

“"The weather reporter looks at the sky’s clues and tells us the plan: rain or sun, warm or cold, windy or calm. We listen to the forecast, then we get ready — the right clothes, the right bag, the right day."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "A weather forecast is the sky’s plan, told to us before it happens."
  2. Read the picture: the presenter in a yellow blazer points at a big weather map, a board with two thermometers reading 18 degrees, a rain-cloud board, a rail with a yellow raincoat, a blue jacket and a purple jumper, a "Tomorrow" board with a sun behind a cloud, and a five-day chart from Monday to Friday with sun and cloud icons.
  3. Play icon-reading: show today’s forecast on your phone — sun, cloud or rain? Ask your child to "read" it back to you like a story.
  4. Let the forecast dress you both: rain icon → raincoat and boots; sun icon → sun hat. Make the choice out loud so the reasoning is heard.
  5. crown the family weather reporter: once a week, your child presents the weather — paper-tube microphone, big gestures, the works.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a TV weather presenter in a yellow blazer stands in a studio: she presents a huge weather map with clouds and coloured weather lines, points at a board with two thermometers reading 18°C, shows a board with a big rain cloud and raindrops, stands beside a clothes rail holding a yellow rain jacket, a blue jacket and a purple jumper, points to a "Tomorrow" card showing a sun behind a cloud, and presents a weekly chart — Monday sunny, Tuesday rain, Wednesday cloud, Thursday partly sunny, Friday sunny — with a temperature number under each day.

Ask your child

"What does the weather reporter tell us?" "What do we take outside if the forecast says rain?" "What does the sun icon mean?" "Did yesterday’s forecast get it right?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The forecast says rain — boots please!" or deliver a full bulletin: "Today is cloudy, tomorrow is sunny — that is the weather, thank you!"

Out in the real world

Make the morning forecast check a fixed ritual — while shoes go on, the sky’s plan gets read. Let your child spot forecast icons on phones, roadside signs, newspapers and TV. After big-weather days, hold the verdict together: right sky, wrong sky, half right?

Try it together

Weather studio: a cardboard TV frame, a paper-tube microphone and yesterday’s drawings as props — your child presents today, tomorrow and "the weekend", complete with sound effects. Then the forecast-vs-reality chart: two columns, sticker for every correct call.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who tells us the sky’s plan? What do we grab when the forecast says rain? What do we do when a big storm is forecast?" Reporter, raincoat, stay home together — planning is now a family skill.

Parent tips

Never pretend forecasts are perfect — the misses are teachable gold: "The sky changed its mind; even weather scientists keep learning." And keep the ritual tiny: one icon, one clothing choice, ten seconds. Rituals that survive are rituals that stay small.

Staying safe

Teach the storm-warning response explicitly: when grown-ups say a big storm is coming, we stay indoors, away from windows, and let the wild sky pass. Children can help — fetching the torch, counting the batteries — because helping prepares, and preparing calms.

This lesson pairs with the Weather Forecast flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Sunny Day — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson defines the sunny day your child already loves, then upgrades it: shadows to chase, shade hunts to run, and the hat-water-shade routine that keeps the whole day comfortable from breakfast to bath.

What is this?

A sunny day is a day when the sun lights the sky almost without clouds: blue above, bright light below, sharp shadows everywhere, and warm ground underfoot from mid-morning on.

What does it mean?

Sunny days have a rhythm. Morning sun is gentle and shadows are long; midday sun is strong and shadows shrink; evening sun cools and shadows stretch again. Families who read that rhythm play outside in the easy hours and rest in shade at the peak.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three sunny-day ideas: sun makes light, warmth and shadows; the midday sun is the strongest, so shade and hats matter most then; and a sunny-day kit — hat, water bottle, sunscreen from a grown-up — goes with us every time.

Why this matters

The sunny day is the strongest cause-and-effect classroom outdoors: stand in light, warm; step into shade, cool; jump, and the shadow jumps. Children who plan around the sun learn that routines are tools, not rules — and they own those tools by age five.

What it teaches

Time-of-day concepts tied to felt experience, spatial reasoning through shadow play, planning and self-care routines, heat awareness, and the pure gross-motor joy of a full outdoor day spent well.

Words to learn

sunnyshadowshademiddaybrightsun hatwater bottlecool

Say this to your child

“"A sunny day means the sun is lighting everything up. We wear our hats, we drink water, we play in the shade when the sun is at its strongest — and our shadows play with us all day long."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "A sunny day is when the sun lights up everything — the sky, the ground, our shadows."
  2. Read the picture: the park ranger shades her eyes to check the sky, adjusts her wide hat, drinks from a water bottle, plays resting in the shade of a big tree, squeezes sunscreen onto her hand and points at a forecast board showing three days — sunny, partly cloudy, cloudy.
  3. Do the shadow check right now: jump — did your shadow jump? Stand still — did it freeze? The sun is the puppeteer.
  4. Run a shade hunt: find three cool resting spots in the garden or park, and name which one you would pick at midday.
  5. Build the routine into a chant: hat on, bottle filled, sunscreen by a grown-up — then out to play. Chant it at the door, every sunny morning.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a park ranger in a khaki hat and uniform: shades her eyes with one hand beneath a bright sun, adjusts her hat brim under a tree, drinks from a blue bottle, rests happily against a big shady trunk, squeezes sunscreen from a bottle with a yellow cap onto her arm, and points at a "Today’s Forecast" board with three columns — a sunny 82, a partly cloudy 76 and a cloudy 70.

Ask your child

"What does the sun do on a sunny day?" "When are our shadows longest — morning or midday?" "Where is the best shade spot?" "What goes in our sunny-day kit?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "My shadow is longer than me now!" "Midday shade time — then back out to play," or recite the door chant unprompted: "Hat, bottle, sunscreen!"

Out in the real world

Track the family shadow on the walk to school across a whole week. Notice who else uses shade: dogs under benches, market stalls under canopies, cafés with umbrellas. Check the forecast board or app together and rate tomorrow’s sunny chances.

Try it together

Shadow circus: make your shadow into a rabbit, a giant, a crab — hands and feet tell the story. Shadow hopscotch: jump only on shady patches. Sundial snack: mark a biscuit-tin shadow with a stone at breakfast, check it again at lunch — the sun moved the shadow, and the snack tastes better outside anyway.

Understanding check

Ask: "What three things does a sunny day give us?" (Light, warmth, shadows.) "What do we do at midday?" (Shade and hats.) "What is in our sunny-day kit?" — Three routines named, one lesson landed.

Parent tips

Anchor the routine to the felt difference, not the lecture: one moment hatless in the sun, then hat on — "cooler, right?" The body remembers what the mouth explains. And never skip your own hat; the routine holds only if grown-ups visibly obey it too.

Staying safe

The midday sun is the strongest — shade rests and plenty of water in the peak hours, sunscreen applied by a grown-up before the day starts, never a stare upward, and never anyone left in a parked car, not even for one minute.

This lesson pairs with the Sunny Day flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Cloudy Day — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson gives the cloudy day its due: what the grey ceiling really is, how the light and shadows change, and the perfectly-cool outdoor jobs — planting, watering, walking — that grey days are secretly best for.

What is this?

A cloudy day is when clouds cover most or all of the sky. The light turns soft and silvery, shadows fade to faint smudges, and the air often feels cooler because the sunshine is filtered through the cloud blankets.

What does it mean?

Cloudy does not automatically mean rainy — clouds have stages: a few white visitors, a half-grey sky, full grey cover, and the heavy dark kind that drips. Reading which stage the sky is in decides the day: coat, no coat, or umbrella in the bag.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three cloudy-day ideas: clouds filter the sun and soften the light; cloudy is not always rainy — we check which grey it is; and cloudy days are cool-work days, perfect for gardens and long walks.

Why this matters

The cloudy day teaches nuance — the sky has more than two settings. Grading the cloud cover (a bit, a lot, all of it) builds observation on a scale, and the reframe "grey days are garden days" widens a child’s idea of which days are good days.

What it teaches

Observation on a gradient, comparison vocabulary, the shadow experiment in reverse (soft light, faint shadows), care-of-plants routines, and emotional reframe practice — finding the good in a quietly grey day.

Words to learn

cloudygreysoft lightcoverdrizzlegardenmildgloomy

Say this to your child

“"The clouds have covered the sky like a big grey blanket. The sun is still up there, resting behind them. Cloudy days are cool and soft — the garden loves them, and so do gardeners. Let us check: is today a cloudy day or a rainy day?"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "A cloudy day is when the clouds pull their blankets over the whole sky."
  2. Read the picture: the gardener in a yellow hat and green jacket stands with her spade under big grey-white clouds while the circles show her looking at clouds, watering plants, zipping a light jacket, holding a thermometer, planting seeds and talking about rain with a little rain cloud in her thought bubble.
  3. Grade today’s sky together: a few clouds, half covered, or all grey? Give the sky a cloud score from one to ten.
  4. Do the shadow check: on full cloud, shadows go faint — the sun’s light is arriving gently, from everywhere at once.
  5. Choose one grey-day job: watering the plants, planting seeds or a long cool walk — then go and do it, wellies standing by in case.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a gardener in a wide yellow hat, green jacket and green boots stands holding a spade in a garden with raised beds and a wooden fence, under a sky full of grey-white clouds. Around her in circles: she looks up at the clouds, waters flowers with a blue watering can, zips her light jacket, holds up a thermometer, plants seeds in a wooden tray, and talks about rain — a small rain cloud floats in her thought bubble.

Ask your child

"What do the clouds do to the sunshine today?" "Is a cloudy day always a rainy day?" "What happened to our shadows?" "What jobs are perfect for a grey day?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The sky has its grey blanket on!" "Shadows are hiding today," or the gardener’s report: "I watered the whole flower bed and I was not even hot."

Out in the real world

Compare feelings across weathers: what does the street look like on a cloudy day versus a sunny one? Notice the cool-work crowd — gardeners, dog walkers, builders — who get on with it happily under grey. Keep the daily cloud score going for a week.

Try it together

Grey-day picnic: the same blanket, the same sandwiches, just softer light — normalise outdoor joy under cloud. Play shadow-hide-and-seek: on a cloudy day nobody can see the seekers’ shadows, a genuinely different game. Then plant something — grey and cool is prime planting weather.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do clouds do to the light? Does cloudy always mean rainy? Name one perfect cloudy-day job." Soft light, not always, and any honest garden answer — the grey day is now a good day.

Parent tips

Watch your own weather talk: children hear everything, and "grey old day" teaches grey means gloomy. Try "soft day" or "good garden weather" and let the reframe do quiet work. And keep the jacket rule honest — cloudy air is often cooler than it looks.

Staying safe

Grey skies still let sun through — for long midday outings, the hat stays in the bag and on the head. And check whether the grey is heading for rain: a heavy, darkening sky means the coat — maybe the umbrella — comes along too.

This lesson pairs with the Cloudy Day flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Rainy Day — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson owns the rainy day end to end: what the sky is doing, the get-ready sequence that keeps everyone dry, the postal worker’s trick for protecting precious things, and the puddle etiquette that makes splashing a joy.

What is this?

A rainy day is when the clouds drop their water steadily over the neighbourhood: grey skies, dripping trees, growing puddles, shiny roads and the whole world smelling of wet stone and green things.

What does it mean?

Rainy days are preparation days — the families who get ready in the right order stay dry and cheerful, and the rain becomes a background drum instead of a day-ruiner. Rain also has jobs: it waters everything, washes the streets and refills the puddle supply.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three rainy-day ideas: rainy days ask for the gear sequence — raincoat, boots, umbrella; precious things stay dry in bags and plastic sleeves; and puddles are for polite splashing — small ones yes, road-side ones never.

Why this matters

The rainy day is a sequencing gym: coat before boots or boots before coat? Zip before hood or hood before zip? Every wet morning rehearses ordering, and the payoff is immediate — the child who dresses right stays warm, dry and proud all the way to the door.

What it teaches

Sequencing and self-dressing mastery, responsibility for belongings (the dry letter!), sensory vocabulary for rain sounds, judgement calls about puddles and roads, and the emotional shift from "rain ruins play" to "rain changes play".

Words to learn

rainyumbrellaraincoatbootspuddlesplashdripsoak

Say this to your child

“"It is a rainy day, so we follow the rain plan: raincoat zipped, boots on, umbrella up. Our precious things ride in a dry bag. We walk carefully near roads, and the small puddles in the garden are all ours to splash."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "A rainy day is the clouds watering the whole town — and we have our rain plan."
  2. Read the picture: the postal worker walks under a big navy umbrella past wet houses; the small panels show him opening the umbrella, zipping a yellow raincoat, pulling on yellow boots, pointing at a puddle, sliding a letter into a clear plastic sleeve to keep it dry, and checking a phone forecast that reads 12 degrees.
  3. Build the sequence together: coat first, then boots, then umbrella last — because the umbrella needs a hand for the door.
  4. Teach the keep-things-dry trick: precious things ride in bags or plastic sleeves, just like the letter on the card. What would YOUR child protect from the rain?
  5. Set the puddle rules with a smile: splash the small garden puddles, step around the kerb-side ones, and never — never — splash towards a road.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a postal worker in a navy cap and light-blue shirt carries a navy mail bag: the big picture shows him walking under a wide navy umbrella on a wet street with houses and a white picket fence; the smaller panels show him opening the folded umbrella, zipping a bright yellow raincoat, pulling on yellow rain boots, crouching to point at a puddle, sliding a letter into a clear plastic sleeve, and holding a phone showing a rain-cloud forecast at 12°C.

Ask your child

"What comes first — the coat or the umbrella?" "How do we keep precious things dry?" "Which puddles are for splashing?" "What is the rain doing for the garden today?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Coat, boots, umbrella — in that order!" "My letter goes in the dry bag," or the puddle verdict: "That one is a splasher, that one is a monster — we step around it."

Out in the real world

Watch the rain workers: postal carriers, delivery riders, road crews — all dressed for it, all still smiling. Notice what the rain feeds on the walk: thirsty flower beds, full gutters singing, the birdbath brimming. Start a rain bowl on the windowsill — outside, lid off — and measure the night’s catch.

Try it together

Rain-band: wooden spoons on pots, rice in a bottle, fingers on windows — which instrument sounds most like the rain outside? Dry-boat regatta: paper boats race along a gutter’s edge (grown-up pace, shallow water). And the classic rainy-day shelter: a blanket fort with a book and a bowl of snacks while the real rain drums on the roof.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the rain plan? How do we keep special things dry? Which puddles may we splash?" Coat-boots-umbrella, bags-and-sleeves, garden-only — the rainy day is now an owned day.

Parent tips

Keep the gear at child height by the door — independence dies on a high hook. Let your child own one piece completely (the umbrella choice, the boot colour). And join the splash: one dignified grown-up stomp in a garden puddle buys a year of rainy-day cooperation.

Staying safe

Wet roads make cars slower to stop — hands held at crossings, walking feet on shiny pavements, never any splashing towards the road. Watch for slippery leaves and painted lines, keep umbrella tips away from eyes, and come home to dry clothes before the shivers start.

This lesson pairs with the Rainy Day flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Stormy Day — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson takes the fear out of the sky’s loudest weather: what lightning and thunder really are, why the boom follows the flash, and the three storm rules from the card’s own poster — plus a thunder-counting game that makes waiting a sport.

What is this?

A stormy day brings dark towering clouds, heavy rain, strong wind, flashes of lightning and rumbles of thunder, all together. It is the sky at its most dramatic — and it usually passes quickly.

What does it mean?

Lightning is a giant spark of electricity jumping inside or between clouds. Thunder is the sound of that spark super-heating the air. Light travels faster than sound, so we always see the flash first and hear the boom afterwards.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three storm ideas: lightning is a giant sky spark and thunder is its sound; the flash comes first and the boom chases it; and our storm plan is the poster’s three rules — stay inside, stay away from trees, stay away from plugs and wires.

Why this matters

Storm fear is among the most common childhood fears — and among the most reducible. Naming the order (flash, count, boom) converts a mystery into a countable game; the poster’s rules give the body a script; and a cosy den gives the feelings somewhere warm to sit.

What it teaches

Sequencing (flash → count → boom), counting under mild excitement, fear-processing through play and explanation, family-safety scripting, and the deep reassurance of routines that hold even when the sky does not.

Words to learn

stormlightningthundersparkrumbleinsidesafecosy

Say this to your child

“"A storm makes big flashes and loud rumbles. The flash is lightning — a giant spark — and the boom is thunder, chasing right after it because sound runs slower than light. We stay inside, away from windows, and watch the show together from our cosy spot."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "A storm is a big cloud having a very loud day — and we watch it from our safe, cosy inside."
  2. Read the picture: the scientist watches a lightning flash from her window, listens for thunder with a hand to her ear, reads in an armchair by a lamp, closes the window latch, checks a storm forecast on a tablet and points at a storm-safety poster that says: stay inside, stay away from trees, stay away from plugs and wires.
  3. Teach the order with hands: flash (fingers flick), count (one-Mississippi, two-Mississippi…), BOOM (stamp). The longer the count, the farther away the storm.
  4. Walk the three rules as a little march: inside! away from trees! away from plugs! Then draw them as a family poster.
  5. Build the storm plan: when the forecast says storm, we shut windows, bring in the cushions and make the den — the storm is the TV tonight.

Look closer at the picture

This stormy card keeps a scientist with glasses and a white lab coat indoors: she watches a fork of lightning over dark rooftops through the window, cups her hand behind her ear to catch the thunder, reads a blue book in an armchair beside a glowing lamp, turns the window latch shut against the rain, points at a tablet with a storm-cloud forecast, and presents a "Storm Safety" poster with three picture rules — a house for stay inside, a crossed-out tree for stay away from trees, and a crossed-out plug for stay away from plugs and wires.

Ask your child

"Which comes first — the flash or the boom?" "What is thunder the sound of?" "Name the three storm rules." "What is our family’s cosy storm spot?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might chant the rules as a march: "Inside! No trees! No plugs!" count the flash-to-boom gap proudly, or declare mid-storm: "The storm is far — the count was BIG."

Out in the real world

Watch how the neighbourhood answers storms: windows closing, market stalls packing up, buses easing along, then everyone back out after. Point to lightning rods and safe buildings — grown-ups have been outsmarting storms for centuries, and the house is on our side.

Try it together

Thunder theatre: flash the lights off, count together, then drum the sofa for thunder — count loud storms in real time from the den. Storm-den night: cushions, torch, picture books about weather, cocoa. The goal is positive association: storms end in dens, cocoa and stories, every single time.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is lightning? Why do we hear thunder after the flash? What are the storm rules?" A sky spark, sound runs slower, and the three-rule march — fear has officially become knowledge.

Parent tips

Your calm is the lesson — narrate your own steadiness: "There is the flash… here comes the count… boom!" If your child is storm-shy, let them control the exposure: den flap open or shut, torch on or off, watching or just listening. Control is the antidote to fear, and cocoa helps.

Staying safe

Storm rules for small people, from the card itself: stay inside, away from windows; stay away from trees — never shelter under one; stay away from plugs and wires during the loudest part. If outside when a storm starts, come in at once — the sky gets the whole stage.

This lesson pairs with the Stormy Day flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Windy Day — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson takes the breeze your child already knows and turns the dial to windy: how a windy day differs, what the wind moves and shakes, the hat-and-window preparations, and the step-by-step joy of flying a kite in an open field.

What is this?

A windy day is when the air moves strongly enough to grab attention: hair streaming sideways, trees swaying, washing snapping, leaves skittering and windows humming. Windy is the breeze’s big sister — same air, more push.

What does it mean?

Strong wind has real power: it bends whole trees, blows hats into next week and rattles doors. It also does glorious things — lifts kites, flies flags, races clouds. The windy-day skill is respect plus enjoyment: secure the loose things, then go feel the force.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three windy-day ideas: windy means the air pushes hard enough to move lots of things; we secure hats, windows and light objects before playing; and windy days are kite days — in open spaces, away from roads and wires.

Why this matters

A windy day is felt physics: your child leans into the push, watches leaves fly and feels a kite tug the string. Cause and effect become whole-body — run and the kite climbs, stop and it dips — and the safety habits (secured hats, shut windows) are rehearsals for real storm readiness.

What it teaches

Physical force awareness, preparation routines (hat straps, window checks), kite-handling coordination, observational sorting (what moves fast, what barely sways), and the confidence of playing competently in big weather.

Words to learn

windygustkitesecureflutterswayblowopen field

Say this to your child

“"On a windy day the air pushes hard — it moves leaves, hats and even kites! We strap our hats on, we shut our windows, and then we go out and feel the push. And in a big open field, the wind will lift a kite right up into the sky."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "A windy day is when the wind pushes hard enough to move everything — even us!"
  2. Read the picture: the kite instructor in a blue cap stands on a grassy field flying a blue-and-yellow kite on a long string; the circles show her feeling the wind on her face, holding the string with both hands, watching leaves fly past, pressing her cap on with both hands, closing a window latch, and pointing at a forecast that reads 18 degrees with a windy cloud icon.
  3. Do the loose-things check before any windy outing: hats on with straps, balloons held tight, windows latched at home. What else could the wind take?
  4. Feel the force game: lean forward into the wind with your whole body — the wind is pushing back! Take three steps against it, then let it push you home, giggling.
  5. Fly the kite in order: open field, grown-up launches, child runs holding the string — run and it climbs, slow down and it dips. That tug in the string is the wind, saying hello.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a kite instructor in a light-blue jacket and blue cap flies a blue-and-yellow diamond kite on a white string in the middle of a grassy field. The labelled circles show her: feeling the wind with eyes closed and palm up, holding the kite string with both hands, watching two green leaves blow through the air, pressing her cap down with both hands, closing a window latch, and pointing at a "TODAY" forecast card with a windy cloud icon reading 18°C.

Ask your child

"What is the wind moving today?" "What do we check before a windy walk?" "What happens to the kite when you run? When you stop?" "Where do kites fly — and where never?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The wind pushed me home!" "My hat is strapped, my window is shut," or the kite report: "I ran and the wind pulled the string — I could FEEL it!"

Out in the real world

Watch the wind workers after a windy night: flags worn out, bins moved, branches down, kites patched. Notice which things sway safely (trees, lamps) and which things should never sway (cranes, wobbly fences). Secure-the-garden becomes a windy-day ritual: balls in, cushions in, trampoline tied.

Try it together

Wind gauge: hold out different papers — tissue, napkin, card — and rank which the wind moves fastest. Sock-in-the-air relay. Then the main event, the kite: practise the run indoors with a ribbon, then take the real kite to the biggest open space you can find. The tug on that string is the whole lesson in one feeling.

Understanding check

Ask: "What kind of day is it when the wind pushes hard? What do we strap on? Where do kites fly?" Windy, hats, open fields far from wires — your child now reads big wind like a local.

Parent tips

Do the preparations as a duo, out loud, every windy time: "Hats? Strapped. Windows? Shut. Loose toys? In the box." The chant becomes the child’s own pre-wind checklist. And manage the down draft: windy-day tiredness is real — big air days end with big snacks and early baths.

Staying safe

Windy-day rules: strap the hat, latch the windows, bring in the light things. Walk clear of old trees, scaffolding and building sites where the wind shakes things loose. Kites fly in open fields only — never near roads, power lines or cables — and the launch is always a grown-up job.

This lesson pairs with the Windy Day flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Snowy Day — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson choreographs the snowy day from first look out the window to the cocoa return: what the white world is doing, the dressing order that keeps it fun, the penguin walk for icy patches, and the jobs — snowploughs! — that keep the town moving.

What is this?

A snowy day is when snow falls and settles: white roofs, white paths, footprints telling who went where, and a special hush because fresh snow softens every sound in the street.

What does it mean?

Snowy days change how everything works: walking slows, cars crawl or stop, schools sometimes close, and big machines come out to help — snowploughs push the snow aside so buses and ambulances can get through.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three snowy-day ideas: snowy days ask for the full kit in order — coat, hat, gloves, boots; icy paths need penguin steps, tiny and careful; and we never walk or play near a working snowplough — we watch from far away with a grown-up.

Why this matters

A snowy day is the year’s biggest routine test: five garments, one order, cold consequences. Mastering it feels enormous to a four-year-old. Add the neighbourhood drama of the snowplough and the sheer joy of the first angel, and the day teaches preparation, patience and celebration at once.

What it teaches

Multi-step sequencing under excitement, balance and body control on slippery ground, community awareness (the plough keeps the town open), patience in dressing, and the pure sensory richness of the year’s most different-feeling day.

Words to learn

snowysnowploughfootprintshushicybootsglovessnow angel

Say this to your child

“"A snowy day turns everything white and quiet. We dress in order — coat, scarf, hat, gloves, boots — then we walk like penguins on the slippery bits. We watch the snowplough from far away while it clears the road, and when the snow is fresh and soft, we make a snow angel."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "A snowy day turns the whole street white and quiet — and we have our snow plan."
  2. Read the picture: the snowplough driver in a yellow high-visibility coat zips it up, wraps a navy scarf, pulls on gloves, drives an orange snowplough with a big shovel pushing snow, lies in the snow making a snow angel, and points at a forecast reading minus 2 degrees.
  3. Drill the dressing order like a song: coat, then scarf, then hat, then gloves, boots last — boots last so nobody skates across the hallway.
  4. Practise penguin steps on the spot: tiny steps, feet flat, knees soft, arms out for balance. Now cross the "icy patch" (a rug) without a wobble.
  5. Make the angel: fall gently backward — a sit, then a soft plop — sweep arms up-down, legs in-out, stand up without stepping on the wings, and admire it from above like the picture.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a snowplough driver with a beard, navy beanie and a yellow high-visibility winter coat: zips the coat to his chin, wraps a navy scarf around his neck, pulls on a navy glove, sits in the cab of an orange snowplough with amber lights pushing a mound of snow with its front shovel, lies spread-eagle in fresh snow next to a swept snow-angel shape, and points at a tablet showing snowflake icons and minus 2 degrees.

Ask your child

"What does a snowy day look and sound like?" "What is the dressing order?" "How do we walk on icy paths?" "What does the snowplough do — and how close do we go?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Coat, scarf, hat, gloves, boots — boots LAST!" "Penguin steps on the ice," or the angel review: "Mine has big wings — I did double arm sweeps!"

Out in the real world

Compare the street before and after the plough passes: where does the snow go? Which paths get gritted? Point out the real helpers — drivers, gritters, post — who keep the town running in the white. And count the bird tracks in fresh snow: the early birds signed their names.

Try it together

Footprint zoo: walk like different animals in fresh snow and guess each other’s prints. Snow-kitchen round two with muffin trays and spoons. The angel gallery: make a whole family of angels — big, small, and teddy-sized — then photograph the flock from a window before the next flurry files it all smooth.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we put on first? How do we walk on ice? How close do we stand to a snowplough?" Coat-first, penguin steps, and very far away — the snowy day is fully choreographed.

Parent tips

Set the warm-up rhythm before the first mittened step: one outside block, one inside warm-up, repeat. Wet gloves go straight on the radiator, dry ones on. And savour the hush yourself — the child who hears you say "listen how quiet" learns that weather is also something to hear.

Staying safe

Full kit every time — wet plus cold chills fast, and wet gloves get swapped, not endured. Penguin steps on ice, never running on shiny ground. Snowploughs are watched from far away with a grown-up, never followed or touched, and inside we go when the shivers start.

This lesson pairs with the Snowy Day flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Foggy Day — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson explains the day the world goes milky: what fog is, how far it lets us see, why bright colours and lights matter, and the walking rules — slow steps, held hands, known paths — that make a foggy day an adventure instead of a worry.

What is this?

Fog is a cloud that forms at ground level — millions of tiny water drops floating in the air right where we walk. It scatters the light so that far-away things fade to grey ghosts and then vanish.

What does it mean?

Fog changes how we use our senses: eyes lose their long range, so ears, memory and bright colours do more work. Everything familiar looks strange, distances are hard to judge, and everyone — walkers, drivers, cyclists — slows down and doubles their looking.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three fog ideas: fog is a cloud down at ground level that hides far things; in fog we make ourselves easy to see — bright coats, lights — and walk slowly; and the fog rule of rules: stay close to your grown-up, on paths you know.

Why this matters

Fog is the rare weather that teaches sensory switching — from eyes to ears — plus the deep safety habit of visibility. A child who understands "I must be seen and stay close" in fog carries the same skill into dusk, car parks and crowded places for life.

What it teaches

Sensory adaptation (listening more, looking closer), distance judgement, colour-and-visibility reasoning, self-restraint at crossings, and the comfort of routine — same streets, same holds, slower pace, still safe.

Words to learn

fogmistmilkyvisibilitybrightflashlightslowlyvanish

Say this to your child

“"Fog is a cloud that floats down low, right where we walk. It hides things that are far away, so we wear something bright, walk slowly, hold hands and use our ears as well as our eyes. The crossing guard helps us — in fog, everyone looks after everyone."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Fog is a cloud that came down to walk the streets with us."
  2. Read the picture: the crossing guard in a bright yellow high-visibility vest points to it proudly, shines a flashlight into the milky air, walks slowly across a zebra crossing, guides a small child in a green hat by the hand, holds up a stop sign while a car glows faintly behind, and checks a forecast reading 5 degrees.
  3. Play the disappearing game on the real fog: how far can you see before things fade? Count the steps to the nearest tree. Is it farther than yesterday?
  4. Do the bright test: stand five steps away. Which is easier to spot — the grey coat or the yellow one? THAT is why foggy-day coats are bright.
  5. Drill the fog walk: my hand, your hand; small steps; eyes AND ears working; cross only at the crossing where the guard helps.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a crossing guard in a navy cap and a bright yellow high-visibility vest: points at the words on the vest, shines a lit flashlight that glows in the milky air, walks slowly across a zebra crossing, holds the hand of a small child in a green bobble hat and teal coat, lifts a red stop sign while a car’s headlights glow softly through the fog behind, and points at a tablet showing a cloud icon and 5°C.

Ask your child

"What is fog made of?" "Why do we wear bright colours in fog?" "What do our ears do on a foggy walk?" "What is the most important fog rule of all?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "We are walking inside a cloud!" "Bright coats so cars can see us," or the rule, word perfect: "Stay close, hold hands, known paths."

Out in the real world

Watch the fog change your own street: the house you can see, the one you cannot, the bus that arrives like a ghost. Spot the fog workers — guards in bright vests, cars with lights on, ferries and trains sounding their horns. Fog dissolves by mid-morning: check the same view at lunch and celebrate the returning rooftops.

Try it together

Fog-game at home: greaseproof paper over a toy binoculars’ ends — how much can you spot now? Bright-survey in the wardrobe: which jackets would a foggy day love? Listening-walk with eyes closed (safely, sitting): what do your ears catch that your eyes missed? Then the torch test at dusk: one light on, one light off — which grown-up gets spotted first?

Understanding check

Ask: "What is fog? Why bright coats? What do we never do in fog?" A ground cloud, to be seen, and run-off-or-wander-off — the fog rules are now family rules.

Parent tips

Keep fog explanations matter-of-fact and slightly magical — "walking inside a cloud" beats "limited visibility" every time. And if fog feels spooky, rehearse the route in sunshine first: the child who knows the three trees and the red door walks fog with confidence, because memory holds the map the mist hides.

Staying safe

Fog rules: stay together — hand in hand on known paths; wear or carry something bright; listen for cars you cannot see and cross only where a guard or clear view helps; never wander off to explore the greyness. Flashlights and reflective bits come out at dawn-and-dusk fog.

This lesson pairs with the Foggy Day flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Hot Weather — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson gives your child the hot-weather playbook: what the heat does to bodies, the drink-rest-shade routine that keeps play going all summer, the splashy ways to cool down, and the signals — dizzy, headachy — that always mean grown-up, now.

What is this?

Hot weather is when the air stays high-and-hot for days: strong sun overhead, warm wind, hot pavements, and everyone seeking shade, water and the cool side of the pillow.

What does it mean?

Bodies work harder in heat — they sweat to stay cool, and sweating uses up water fast. That is why hot days rewrite the routine: more drinks, slower midday, lighter clothes, cooler games. The heat is not the enemy; running dry is.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three hot-weather ideas: hot bodies need water many times a day, not just when thirsty; the midday sun is the strongest, so shade and rests live at the middle of the day; and any dizzy, headachy or sick feeling means stop and tell a grown-up straight away.

Why this matters

Hot weather is the first weather that can genuinely make a small body unwell, which makes it the most important self-care lesson in the class. A child who owns the drink-rest-shade routine — and knows that telling a grown-up about feeling unwell is brave, not whiny — carries a lifelong skill.

What it teaches

Interoception (reading one’s own body signals), routine planning around the sun, honest reporting as bravery, water-science through evaporation play, and the social rules of water safety that summer always rehearses.

Words to learn

hotshadehydratesweatcool downdizzysunscreenmidday

Say this to your child

“"When the weather is very hot, we help our bodies: water many times a day, light clothes and a sun hat, rests in the shade when the sun is strongest, and cool water play with a grown-up watching. If anyone feels dizzy or unwell in the heat, we stop and tell a grown-up right away."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Hot weather means our bodies need extra help to stay cool and happy."
  2. Read the picture: the lifeguard by the pool wears a red sun hat, drinks from a big blue bottle, rubs sunscreen from an SPF 50 bottle onto his face, rests in the shade in a white chair, gives a thumbs-up from the pool wearing sunglasses, and holds a thermometer reading 30 degrees.
  3. Set the routine as three anchors: WATER often — bottle in hand, refills cheered; REST in shade when the sun is highest; HAT and sunscreen before the door.
  4. Teach the body signals with respect: dizzy, headachy, sick-in-the-heat means sit down, sip water, tell a grown-up immediately — that is not complaining, that is top-class body care.
  5. Plan one proper cool-down: paddling pool, water table, or a swim where a grown-up and a lifeguard are watching — always watching.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a lifeguard in a white shirt and red shorts works at a sunny pool: he puts on a wide-brimmed red hat marked LIFEGUARD, drinks from a big blue water bottle, rubs sunscreen from a yellow SPF 50 bottle onto his cheek, relaxes in a white chair in the shade of a big umbrella, stands chest-deep in the pool giving a thumbs-up in dark sunglasses, and holds a white thermometer reading 30° with a little sun on it.

Ask your child

"What do our bodies need lots of on hot days?" "Where do we rest at midday?" "What does sunscreen do — and who puts it on?" "What do we say if we feel dizzy in the heat?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Water break!" unprompted at the park, "Midday is shade time," or the brave line practised once and kept forever: "I feel dizzy — I need a grown-up."

Out in the real world

Spot the heat routines all around: dogs stretched in shade, shop awnings out, the paddling pool in every second garden, the ice-cream queue. Feel the science: sun-side versus shade-side of a wall, hot car roof versus cool grass. Refill stations — which fountains and taps are on your walking map?

Try it together

Water-wall: cups, sponges and buckets against a fence — transfer games that soak everyone equally. Ice-rescue: freeze small toys in a tub and free them with warm water and spoons. Shade-fort build for the midday hours. Then the classic: a proper run under the sprinkler, towels on the line afterwards like signal flags.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do hot bodies need? Where do we rest at midday? What do we say if we feel dizzy?" Water, shade, and grown-up-right-away — the heat is now managed, not feared.

Parent tips

Make drinking silly, not dutiful — silly-straw races, tick-charts, cheers at every refill. Freeze a bottle half-full then top it up for all-day cold. And protect the nap: hot, play-drunk children melt by late afternoon; shade the midday and the evening goes sweet instead of screamy.

Staying safe

Hot-weather rules: water often even without thirst; shade and rests at midday; hat and sunscreen applied by a grown-up; never anyone — child or pet — left in a parked car, not even for a minute; and any dizzy or sick feeling means stop, sit, sip and tell a grown-up at once.

This lesson pairs with the Hot Weather flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Warm Weather — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson names the season children love best: the comfortable middle between cool and hot. What warm weather changes — clothes, windows, routines — and the simple habits (water bottle handy, hat for bright hours) that keep the golden days easy.

What is this?

Warm weather is comfortable mild heat: warmer than cool days, gentler than hot ones. Shirtsleeve and shorts weather, when windows stay open, play moves outdoors and nothing about going outside needs negotiating.

What does it mean?

Warm weather changes whole households: heavier clothes go away, blankets thin out, windows open for fresh air, plants drink more, and the garden becomes the family’s best room. It is the easiest weather to be out in — which is exactly why the small habits still matter.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three warm-weather ideas: warm days ask for light clothes; houses get fresh air with open windows — feet stay on the floor near low ones; and the water bottle comes to every game, because warm-air play still drinks the body dry, just slowly.

Why this matters

Warm weather is where weather routines become automatic — the training ground between the drama of hot and cold. A child who keeps the bottle-and-hat habits through the easy season owns them by the time the difficult seasons test them.

What it teaches

Seasonal sorting (what changes when warmth arrives), self-dressing in lighter layers, fresh-air awareness, steady hydration habits, and the observational joy of comparing the same room, the same walk, across two seasons.

Words to learn

warmmildlight clothesfresh airopen windowgardengentleseason

Say this to your child

“"Warm weather means it is easy to be outside — we wear our light clothes, we open the windows for fresh air, we water the flowers in the evening, and we keep our water bottle close while we play, because even easy weather makes us thirsty."”

Step by step
