  1. Show the card: "Warm weather is the comfortable middle — not too hot, not too cold, just right for playing."
  2. Read the picture: the postman in a straw hat and light blue shirt waters pink and yellow flowers with a green can, drinks from his water bottle, opens a window from inside, kicks a football across the lawn, and points at a sunny forecast reading 28 degrees.
  3. Do the wardrobe switch together: which clothes are warm-weather clothes? Let your child sort the drawer — shorts here, jumpers there.
  4. Open the day like the card: window open, air in, plant watered. Feet on the floor by low windows — fresh air yes, climbing no.
  5. Anchor the bottle: warm-weather play still needs water. Bottle lives where the game lives, and refills are cheered.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a postman in a straw hat with a navy band, a light-blue short-sleeve shirt and navy shorts stands in a sunny garden: he adjusts his collar, waters pink and yellow flowers with a green watering can, drinks from a water bottle, opens a window beside a potted plant on the sill, runs kicking a black-and-white football across the grass, and points at a tablet showing a sun icon and 28 degrees.

Ask your child

"What do we wear in warm weather?" "What do we open to let fresh air in?" "What does the garden need more of in warm days?" "What stays with us at every game?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Warm day — shorts day!" "Window open, fresh air coming," or the gardener’s news: "I watered the flowers and the football match continued."

Out in the real world

Track the season’s changes on your own street: lighter clothes on the washing line, open windows up the road, the ice-cream van’s return, longer evenings. Compare photographs of the same walk in winter and in warmth — the trees, the clothes, the light, all different.

Try it together

Warm-evening games: the lawn becomes the stadium — football, skipping, chalk hopscotch, all in golden light. Flower-crew: your child owns the evening watering round with a small can. Window-report: each morning, is today a light-clothes day? The child who reports the season runs the season.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we wear in warm weather? What do we open for fresh air? What comes to every game?" Light clothes, windows, the water bottle — the easy season is now fully managed.

Parent tips

Warm days whisper rather than shout — keep the routines quietly alive: bottle filled, hat for the bright hours, window safety said once and held. And bank the ease: the child who self-manages water and hats in warm weather will re-learn the winter kit twice as fast.

Staying safe

Warm-day rules: water bottle within reach of every game; hat and shade for the brightest midday hours even when the air feels gentle; feet on the floor near open low windows — fresh air, no leaning; and evening watering with a watchful eye so the can waters flowers, not puddles indoors.

This lesson pairs with the Warm Weather flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Cool Weather — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the season between warm and cold: what the fresh nip in the air means, how one good layer solves it, the zip-up skill that makes jackets child-owned, and the honest cheek-check that says when inside is the right answer.

What is this?

Cool weather is fresh, chilly air — noticeably colder than warm, gentler than properly cold. You feel the nip at once, breath may show on the coolest mornings, and one comfortable jacket turns the whole day bright again.

What does it mean?

Cool days are layer days: one zip-up layer, easy to shed when the sun arrives or the game heats up. Moving air makes cool feel cooler still — that is why bike riders and walkers zip right up. Cool weather is the training season for the deep cold to come.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three cool-weather ideas: cool air asks for one good layer — jacket, closed shoes; the zip is the child’s own job and own pride; and cheeks tell the truth — rosy is fine, shivery means inside for a warm-up.

Why this matters

Cool weather is decision practice at the perfect difficulty: one layer, felt results. Zip it and feel warm, unzip when running, choose again tomorrow. That loop — decide, feel, adjust — is self-regulation in its most wearable form.

What it teaches

Self-dressing mastery (the zip!), temperature self-assessment, cause-and-effect with clothing choices, fine-motor control, and the independence glow of managing one’s own comfort.

Words to learn

coolcrispjacketziplayerwarm drinkrosybreeze

Say this to your child

“"Cool weather means the air is fresh and a bit chilly. We wear one good jacket — zipped by me! — and closed shoes. If we get warm playing, we can unzip. When we come home with rosy cheeks, that is the cool air saying we did it right."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Cool weather means the air has a fresh nip — one good jacket makes it perfect."
  2. Read the picture: the bike courier in a blue helmet zips his light blue jacket, ties his blue sneaker laces on a doorstep, holds a little thermometer that reads 72, carries a takeaway cup of warm drink, rides through the neighbourhood in a bike lane and points at a forecast reading 14 degrees.
  3. Learn the zip in stages: bottom teeth together, slider down, hold and pull — practise on the coat, then the jacket, until it is solo.
  4. Do the layer decision together at the door: peek outside, feel the air — jacket today? Which one? Your child picks from the hook.
  5. End with the cheek check on return: rosy and happy means the layer was right; shivery means we learn and layer up more next time.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a bike courier in a blue bike helmet and a blue hooded jacket: zips the jacket up to his chin, crouches on a doorstep tying the laces of his blue trainers, holds up a small thermometer reading 72, carries a warm drink in a takeaway cup, rides his bicycle along a road with a painted bike lane, and points at a tablet forecast showing a partly-sunny icon and 14 degrees.

Ask your child

"What does cool air feel like?" "How many layers does a cool day need?" "Show me how your zip works." "What do rosy cheeks tell us?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Cool day — one layer!" "I zipped it all by myself," or the walk report: "My cheeks went rosy and I had a warm drink."

Out in the real world

Feel the cool-air difference on a bike or a fast buggy ride — moving air is colder air. Watch the zip-workers: riders, walkers, runners all zipping at the door. Keep the thermos ritual: one warm walk a week makes cool weather the cosy season.

Try it together

Zip-school: races on your own jacket, then helping teddy with his. Layer-sort relay: which clothes are cool-day clothes, which are cold-day ones? Warm-walk club: thermos of warm drink, crunchy leaves, and the mirror check at home — rosy cheeks earn the cocoa.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many layers for cool weather? Whose job is the zip? What do rosy cheeks mean?" One layer, mine, and all-is-well — cool weather is now child-managed.

Parent tips

Resist dressing your child in two layers "to be safe" — one good layer with a felt result teaches more than double layers with none. And hand over the zip completely: the first solo zip of the season deserves the same celebration as a lost tooth.

Staying safe

Cool plus wind feels much colder — zip up for rides and walks, fingers covered on the chilliest days. Head in when shivers start; rosy is comfortable, shivery is a signal. And on the coolest mornings, breath-mist spotting is fun — but roads stay for walking, never for playing.

This lesson pairs with the Cool Weather flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Cold Weather — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson takes on the serious cold: what freezing air does to bodies and puddles, how layers hold warmth in, the ice rules that keep small feet safe, and the warm-up routine — blanket, cocoa, radiator — that ends every cold-day outing like the mountain experts do.

What is this?

Cold weather is when the air drops close to or below freezing: breath turns to mist, puddles grow thin ice lids, fingers and ears feel the bite first, and snow may whiten the hills and rooftops.

What does it mean?

Cold air steals body warmth — fastest from the bits that stick out: fingers, ears, noses, necks. Layers trap warm air close to the body, and each extra layer is another blanket of still air. Ice forms when water freezes: shiny, slippery, beautiful — and strictly for looking.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three cold-weather ideas: cold days need many layers — coat, hat, gloves, scarf — because layers hold our warmth; ice is shiny and slippery and never for walking on or touching with tongues; and the routine ends inside — blanket, warm drink, warm-up done.

Why this matters

Cold weather is the deepest self-care lesson in the class: the body signals cold clearly (shivers, clumsy fingers) and the child learns to answer those signals with action — more layers or inside. Reading and answering one’s own body is the skill underneath all health habits.

What it teaches

Layer logic (trapped warm air), body-signal literacy (shivering, numb fingers), ice awareness, dressing sequences under real motivation, and the cosy discipline of the warm-up routine that ends every outing.

Words to learn

coldfrosticelayersshivernumbwarm upthermometer

Say this to your child

“"Cold weather means the air wants to take our warmth, so we wear many layers — coat, hat, gloves, scarf — like blankets we can walk in. Ice is shiny and slippery: we look at it, never stamp it. Then we come in, wrap up and get warm again. That is how cold days work."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Cold weather means the air can make our bodies chilly fast — so we dress deep and warm up well."
  2. Read the picture: the mountain-rescue walker in a red jacket fastens it up, pulls on gloves, wraps a scarf, holds a thermometer reading minus 6, sits warm inside under a blanket with a hot drink by a wood stove, and checks a forecast showing minus 8 with snow.
  3. Build the layer picture with hands: one layer is one blanket of warm air; two layers is two blankets. How many blankets does today need?
  4. Set the ice rule like a rhyme: shiny means slippery — we look, we never lick, we never stamp. Puddles with lids are museum pieces.
  5. Drill the warm-up finish: come in, wet things off, blanket on, warm drink in hands. The outing is not done until the warm-up is done.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a mountain-rescue walker wears a red jacket with white cross patches and a dark beanie: fastens the jacket to the chin, pulls on a dark glove, wraps a navy scarf around the neck, holds a white thermometer reading −6°C, sits warm indoors under a blanket holding a mug beside a wood-burning stove, and points at a forecast tablet reading −8°C with snow icons by a mountain-rescue poster.

Ask your child

"Where does our body feel cold first?" "Why do we wear many layers instead of one big one?" "What is the rule about shiny ice?" "How does a cold-day outing end?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Two layers, two blankets of warm!" "Shiny means slippery — we look, never lick," or announce the finish like the experts: "Blanket, cocoa — warm-up complete!"

Out in the real world

Find the ice on the walk: puddle lids, windscreen frost, the shiny bit of the path the sun has not reached. Watch the layer-workers: builders, posties, dog walkers — all layered deep. Check the thermometer together every morning of the cold snap and let the number pick the number of blankets.

Try it together

Blanket-lab: wrap one teddy in one cloth, another in three — which stays cosiest? That is layers. Ice-look-but-not-touch: find three shiny puddle lids on the walk and rank their shine. Warm-up ritual as a game: wet kit off, blanket burrito, cocoa with two marshmallows — the child who owns the routine owns the season.

Understanding check

Ask: "Why many layers? What do we never do with ice? How does a cold outing end?" Blankets-of-warm, look-never-lick, and blanket-cocoa-warm — the cold now has a system, and the system has your child.

Parent tips

Warm children agree to come inside; cold-stunned ones melt. So set the come-in signals together before the outing: "When your fingers go clumsy or the shivers start, that is your body talking — we listen first time." And keep the warm-up ceremonial: the cocoa is not a snack, it is the finish line.

Staying safe

Cold rules: cover fingers, ears and neck first; come in when shivering starts or fingers go clumsy. Ice is for looking — never for stamping, licking or walking on ponds or frozen water of any kind. Wet clothes get changed the moment we are home. Warm-up is part of the plan, not a treat.

This lesson pairs with the Cold Weather flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Spring — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches spring as a story your child can watch weekly: what the season wakes up, how to adopt a tree and track its changes, how to plant the first seeds, which birds come back to sing — and why the rain jacket never quite goes away.

What is this?

Spring is the season of waking up: days stretch longer and warmer, buds burst into leaves, bulbs push up shoots, blossom covers the trees, and the birds that left for winter return singing and busy with nests.

What does it mean?

Spring is change you can watch at child speed — one week buds, the next week leaves, the week after blossom. It is also a moody season: sunshine, shower, sunshine can share a single hour, which is why spring outings keep a rain jacket folded in the bag.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three spring ideas: spring is when plants wake and grow and birds come home; growth is fast and watchable — track one tree and see the story; and spring weather swings between sun and shower, so the light rain jacket travels with us.

Why this matters

Spring is the season of patient observation: the child who visits the same tree every week learns that big changes are made of small weekly changes — the deepest idea in science, taught by a bud. Add planting a seed and the season teaches cause, patience and care in one pot.

What it teaches

Weekly observation and recording, growth sequencing, plant-care responsibility, bird recognition and listening, weather flexibility (sun-shower-sun in one outing), and the vocabulary of new life: bud, shoot, blossom, nest, shoot, seedling.

Words to learn

springbudblossomseedshootnestshowergrow

Say this to your child

“"Spring is the waking-up season. The trees grow new leaves, the flowers push up, the birds come back to sing and build nests, and we plant our seeds in the soft ground. We keep our rain jackets close, because spring skies love a quick shower between the sunshine."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Spring is when the world wakes up — the trees, the flowers, the birds."
  2. Read the picture: the gardener in a straw hat plants seeds in the soft soil, touches the new green leaves on a branch, wears a yellow rain jacket under a grey shower, watches a robin and a blue bird on a blossom branch, waters the tulips with a green can and points at a partly-sunny forecast reading 18 degrees.
  3. Adopt a tree today: your tree for the whole spring. Visit weekly, draw what changed — bud, leaf, blossom — and keep the drawings in order like a comic strip.
  4. Plant the first seeds: beans in a clear cup by the window. Watch the root wiggle down, the shoot push up. Measure it with your finger every Monday.
  5. Pack the spring bag: sun hat AND folded rain jacket. Say the spring rule out loud: in spring we carry both, because the sky changes its mind.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a gardener in a straw hat with a green band, a light-green shirt and green overalls: kneels to plant seeds beside a seed packet with tulips blooming nearby, reaches up to touch fresh new leaves on a branch, wears a yellow rain jacket under a grey shower cloud, sits on a bench watching a robin and a small blue bird on a blossom branch, waters pink tulips and white daisies with a green watering can, and points at a tablet showing a partly-sunny icon and 18 degrees.

Ask your child

"What is waking up in spring?" "What did OUR tree change this week?" "What does a seed need to start growing?" "Why do we carry a rain jacket in spring?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might report like a scientist: "Two new leaves on our tree — three last week plus one!" or the planting log: "My bean grew a shoot as tall as my finger."

Out in the real world

Walk the neighbourhood as a bud-census: which trees woke first? Count the returning birds and learn one song by heart — the one that sings outside your window. Find the first bees back at work on the blossom and watch them a respectful moment: spring has staff, and they are busy.

Try it together

Tree-diary comic strip: one square per week, taped in a row — the tree’s whole spring as a story. Seed race: bean versus sunflower in neighbouring cups — who sprouts first, who grows tallest? Nest-watch from a distance with binoculars: busy birds, never touched, always marvellous.

Understanding check

Ask: "What happens in spring? What are we tracking on our tree? Why carry a rain jacket?" Waking-up, the weekly changes, and moody skies — your child is now fluent in spring.

Parent tips

Keep the tree visits short and sacred — five minutes, same tree, same question: "What changed?" The discipline is the magic. And when the shower ambushes your picnic, laugh and shelter: getting caught by a spring shower once teaches the jacket rule better than a hundred reminders.

Staying safe

Spring rules: hats return with the blossom — spring sunshine still burns; wash hands after soil and watering cans before snacks; watch nests and baby birds from a distance, never touch; and on blossom-branch climbs, remember wet spring grass is slippery grass.

This lesson pairs with the Spring flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Summer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson gives summer its structure: the longest, brightest days, the hat-sunscreen-water routine that never takes a day off, the swim rules that matter most, and how to read a beach flag like a local — all so the golden season stays pure joy.

What is this?

Summer is the warmest season: the longest days and strongest sun, holidays from school, the beach and the pool at their best, fruit ripening everywhere and daylight stretching right into the evening.

What does it mean?

Summer fun runs on summer rules. The sun is strong all day, so hats, sunscreen and shade at midday are how the day works — not optional extras. Swimming happens where lifeguards watch, between the flags. And the long light plays tricks: bedtime says sleep while the sky says play.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three summer ideas: summer sun is strong — hat, sunscreen by a grown-up and water all day, every day; we swim only where a watching grown-up and the lifeguards can see us, between the red-and-yellow flags; and the strongest-sun hours are for shade forts, slow games and long cool drinks.

Why this matters

Summer carries the season’s biggest safety stakes and its biggest joys in the same hours. The child who learns the flag system, the watch-me-swim rule and the midday-shade rhythm at four and five owns them for every summer after — this is the class’s most lasting lesson wearing its happiest face.

What it teaches

Rule ownership (flags, swim-with-a-grown-up), routine persistence through holiday looseness, time concepts through daylight tracking, water confidence with supervision, and the self-knowledge of reading one’s own thirst, heat and tiredness.

Words to learn

summerlifeguardflagsunscreenmiddayshadepaddleripened

Say this to your child

“"Summer is the long, bright, beach season. We wear our hats, we drink water all day, we rest in the shade when the sun is strongest — and we swim only where a grown-up is watching and the red-and-yellow flag says the lifeguards can see us. Then summer is all joy, all season."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Summer is the season of long bright days — and the sun plays by strong rules."
  2. Read the picture: the beach-safety lifeguard in a yellow hat and shirt waves on the sand beside a red-and-yellow flag on a pole and a rescue board; the panels show her adjusting the sun hat, rubbing sunscreen from a bottle, drinking water, swimming in the sea with a small child, resting in a striped chair under an umbrella and pointing at a sunny forecast reading 29 degrees.
  3. Learn the beach flags like treasure signs: red-and-yellow means lifeguards watch this stretch — we swim between the flags, always in sight of our grown-up.
  4. Fix the routine as a song: hat, sunscreen, water bottle — every day, no holidays from the routine, even when the day feels easy.
  5. Plan the midday like the card: the strong-sun hours are for shade — a fort, a striped chair, a long drink — then back out when the sun mellows.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a beach-safety lifeguard in a yellow wide-brim hat and yellow "beach safety" shirt stands waving on the sand: behind her fly a red-and-yellow flag on a pole and a yellow rescue board marked RESCUE, with a lifeguard chair and a striped umbrella nearby; the panels show her adjusting her hat, rubbing sunscreen from a bottle onto her cheek, drinking from a bottle, standing waist-deep in the sea with a small boy, dozing happily in a striped beach chair under an umbrella, and pointing at a phone forecast reading 29° with a sun icon and the word Sunny.

Ask your child

"What do the red-and-yellow flags mean?" "Who watches us when we swim?" "What are the midday hours for?" "What never takes a holiday in summer?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Between the flags, near my grown-up!" "Midday is shade-fort time," or the routine anthem: "Hat, sunscreen, bottle — every day!"

Out in the real world

Read the flags at every beach and pool visit — red-and-yellow for swimming, and ask the lifeguard together what today means. Spot the summer routines on the sand: hats, umbrellas, cool boxes, the lifeguard’s high chair. Track the long light: what time does the sun set this week — and next?

Try it together

Flag-game in the garden: one child waves red-and-yellow — swimming happens "between" two towels, grown-up in the middle. Shade-fort engineering contest for the midday hours. Fruit-ice lolly kitchen: freeze juice with berries. And the summer classic: an evening walk in the golden light, tracking how late the shadows stretch.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do the flags mean? Who watches at swim time? What never takes a summer holiday?" Lifeguards-watch, my-grown-up, and hat-sunscreen-water — the golden season is now safe to love completely.

Parent tips

Hold the routine through the holiday looseness — summer is when routines quietly dissolve, so anchor just three (hat, water, swim-with-a-watching-grown-up) and defend them warmly. And answer "why?" fully once: children follow rules they understand; "so the lifeguard can always see you" beats "because" every time.

Staying safe

Summer’s big rules: never swim without a watching grown-up, only between the flags where lifeguards watch; hats and sunscreen every day, shade at midday; never sit in a parked car; and come to a grown-up at once for any dizzy, headachy or sick feeling in the heat.

This lesson pairs with the Summer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Autumn — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns autumn into the collecting season: why the leaves change and fall, how to build a leaf collection worth keeping, the raking-and-jumping tradition, the sweater switch in the wardrobe — and why autumn wind keeps taking hats.

What is this?

Autumn is the season after summer: days shorten, air cools, and deciduous trees stop making green, letting gold, orange and red show instead — then let the leaves go, one gust at a time.

What does it mean?

Autumn is the great change-and-fall season: leaves stop making their green food, show their hidden colours, then drop to feed the soil. The cooling air asks for sweaters. The season’s winds pick up — which is why autumn walks come with hat-holding.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three autumn ideas: leaves change colour because the tree is resting for winter, then fall to feed the ground; autumn air asks for sweaters and light layers; and autumn wind is playful — hats get held, and leaf heaps get jumped in.

Why this matters

Autumn is the classification season: leaves by colour, shape, size, tree. Sorting a real, beautiful collection is early-maths and early-science in one afternoon. The visible cooling also ties calendar to wardrobe — the child who packs away the summer clothes has understood the season, not just watched it.

What it teaches

Sorting and classifying with real objects, seasonal cause-and-effect (less sun, cooler days, colour change), collection-building and care, wardrobe switching as life-admin practice, and gross-motor joy in raking and jumping.

Words to learn

autumnleafgoldrakesweatergustcrunchharvest

Say this to your child

“"Autumn is the leaf season. The trees turn gold and orange, then let their leaves go — the wind helps them fly. We wear our sweaters, we rake the leaves into heaps, we collect the prettiest ones, and we hold our hats when the autumn wind comes dancing."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Autumn is when the leaves turn gold and orange and fall down for a rest."
  2. Read the picture: the school caretaker in a cap rakes leaves into a heap by the school, wears a light grey sweater, holds up maple leaves in orange and yellow, kneels to collect leaves into a big green bag, holds his cap on in the wind as leaves fly, and points at a forecast reading 15°C.
  3. Start the collection: gather ten fallen leaves — different colours, shapes, sizes. Sort them at the kitchen table: by colour, then size, then shape. Keep the best in a heavy-book press.
  4. Do the sweater switch: which clothes are autumn clothes? Let your child move the summer things away and lay out the jumpers.
  5. Practise hat-holding: autumn wind tests hats. Hand on head at the gusty bits — and if it blows off, we chase it, laughing, and hold on tighter.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a school caretaker in a navy cap, light-grey zip sweater and navy trousers works around a school building: he rakes orange leaves into a heap beside an orange-leafed tree, stands smiling in his sweater, holds up two maple leaves — one orange, one golden — kneels packing leaves into a tall green garden bag, steadies his cap with one hand as leaves swirl past a playground slide, and points at a tablet forecast showing a cloud icon and 15°C.

Ask your child

"Why do the leaves change colour?" "What did we put in our collection today?" "What do we wear now the air is cooler?" "What does the autumn wind love to take?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Our tree went full gold this week!" "Sweater weather — I picked the blue one," or the wind report: "I held my hat with ONE hand — the wind tried!"

Out in the real world

Walk the leaf-line: which trees turned first, which are still green? Find the leaf-workers — caretakers, sweepers, the wind itself. Visit a market or farm at harvest time and name what autumn ripened: apples, pumpkins, plums. Notice the darker mornings — autumn is shortening the days.

Try it together

Leaf-olympics: best colour, biggest, funniest shape, most points. Rake-and-jump: a proper heap, a proper jump, a proper repeat. Leaf-art: rubbings with crayons over the ridges, collages of the collection. And the tree-watch begins: adopt your tree now, so winter’s bare branches are a story, not a surprise.

Understanding check

Ask: "What happens to the leaves in autumn? What do we wear? What does the wind take?" Change-and-fall, sweaters, and hats — the golden season is officially collected.

Parent tips

Let the collection be the child’s — messy, abundant, curated by enthusiasm rather than by adult taste. The heavy-book press is the museum, and the museum belongs to them. And join the jump: one grown-up cannonball into the leaf heap makes the whole season memorable.

Staying safe

Autumn rules: dewy and leafy slopes are slippery — walking feet down leafy banks; shorter, darker days mean something bright on jackets for the roadside walk; and leaf piles at the kerb are never for jumping — garden heaps only, where no traffic passes.

This lesson pairs with the Autumn flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Winter — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson assembles winter the way the card does — coat, scarf, gloves, then the careful outside world: frosty paths walked carefully, bus stops waited in shelter, the early dark noticed — and the blanket-cocoa finish that makes winter feel mastered, not endured.

What is this?

Winter is the coldest season: the shortest days, the longest nights, bare trees, frosty mornings and, in many places, snow and ice. Everyone finds warm ways through — coats and fires for people, dens and thick fur for animals.

What does it mean?

Winter rewrites daily life: dressing takes longer and more layers, walking gets careful on frosty ground, waiting happens in sheltered spots, and the dark arrives early. Winter is also the season of warm returns — the house glows brighter the colder the street.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three winter ideas: winter asks for the full kit — warm coat, scarf, gloves, thick boots — before any door opens; frosty paths need careful small steps; and every winter outing ends with the warm-up: wet things off, warmth on, drink in hands.

Why this matters

Winter is self-care at its most visible: the child who can dress for winter, walk on frost and warm up afterwards has mastered the year’s hardest routine. And the early dark, met with lantern walks and cosy rituals, becomes atmosphere instead of fear.

What it teaches

Full multi-item sequencing, careful motor control on frost, patience with the long dressing routine, day-length awareness (dark at teatime!), and the emotional pattern of effort-then-cosiness that winter teaches best.

Words to learn

winterfrostcoatglovesscarfshelterduskwarm up

Say this to your child

“"Winter is the coldest season, so we wear the full kit — coat, scarf, hat, gloves, boots — before we open any door. We take small careful steps on frosty paths, we wait for the bus in the shelter, and when we come home, we warm up: blanket, cocoa, cosy. That is how winter is done."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Winter is the coldest season — we dress deep and walk careful."
  2. Read the picture: the bus driver in a navy fur-hooded coat fastens it, wraps a long blue scarf, pulls on blue gloves, walks carefully on the snowy pavement past a blue bus, waits with hands in pockets under a "BUS STOP" shelter, and points at a forecast reading TODAY minus 2 degrees with snowflakes.
  3. Drill the full kit in order, every time: coat, then scarf, then hat, then gloves, then boots — each piece named out loud like a roll-call.
  4. Practise the frost walk: small flat steps, knees soft, hands free — on the rug, then on the real path. Shiny means careful.
  5. Build the warm-up finish as a ritual: wet things off, blanket on, warm drink, check the cheeks. Winter outings end in cosiness, always.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a bus driver with curly dark hair wears a navy winter coat with a fur-trimmed hood: fastens the coat with a hand in the pocket, wraps a long blue scarf around her neck, pulls on a blue glove, walks carefully along a snowy pavement with a blue city bus behind, waits calmly with hands in pockets under a bus-stop shelter marked BUS STOP, and points at a tablet reading TODAY with a snow-cloud icon and −2°.

Ask your child

"What is the winter roll-call?" (Coat, scarf, hat, gloves, boots.) "How do we walk on frost?" "Where do we wait for the bus?" "How does every winter outing end?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might run the roll-call solo: "Coat! Scarf! Hat! Gloves! Boots — check!" report the pavement: "Frosty bit — small steps," or declare the finish: "Blanket, cocoa — winter done right."

Out in the real world

Track the season’s signals: darker mornings, darker teatimes, breath-clouds at the bus stop, frost on the grass that melts by lunch. Watch the winter workers — drivers, posties, gritters — keeping the town moving. Notice the animal plans: fat birds at the feeder, cats curled on warm windowsills.

Try it together

Dressing-race against the clock — beat yesterday’s roll-call time. Lantern walk at dusk with a real lantern or torch: make the early dark a treat. Winter den: the blanket fort with books and cocoa where all frosty outings end. And the window-frost gallery: breathe on the glass and draw in the mist.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the winter kit. How do frosty paths get walked? How do outings end?" The full roll-call, small careful steps, and blanket-cocoa — winter is now a routine your child runs.

Parent tips

Keep winter outings short and double-batched: twenty brisk minutes out, full warm-up, and out again if the spirit is willing. The dressing effort is the day’s biggest ask — celebrate the roll-call like a trophy. And make the dark friendly early: lanterns, torches and window-glow turn dusk into winter’s own story-time.

Staying safe

Winter rules: the full kit before every door, no exceptions — fingers, ears and necks chill first. Small steps on frost and ice, never running on shiny ground, ice on ponds strictly for looking. Something bright or reflective for the dark walks, and warm-up inside before the shivers turn to shivers-plus.

This lesson pairs with the Winter flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Umbrella — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson masters the umbrella from fold to fold: naming its parts, the open-outdoors rule, holding it high so it can shed rain, the spoke-safety courtesy for crowded pavements, and the satisfying click of folding it away dry.

What is this?

An umbrella is a folding canopy on a handle: fabric stretched over ribbed spokes that opens into a small round roof and folds back into a slim stick you carry until the rain starts.

What does it mean?

The umbrella works by shedding: rain lands on the sloped fabric and slides off, while you stay dry in the middle. That is why we hold it up high — the roof needs its shape and its height. The spokes that give the roof its curve are also its pointy bits, and they ask for room and respect.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three umbrella ideas: umbrellas open outdoors only, at the doorstep spot; we hold them up high and away from eyes — ours and other people’s; and when the rain ends we fold them carefully and let them dry by the door.

Why this matters

An umbrella is a child’s first piece of equipment with real moving parts and a real safety edge — the spokes. Learning to open, carry and fold it is fine-motor skill, sequencing and courtesy all in one object, and the confidence of carrying your own roof is enormous.

What it teaches

Mechanical sequencing (open, hold, fold), fine-motor control, spatial awareness of sharp points around others, responsibility for equipment, and the social grace of keeping one’s spokes to oneself on a crowded street.

Words to learn

umbrellacanopyspokeshandlefoldshelterrain roofdry

Say this to your child

“"The umbrella is our own little rain roof. We open it outdoors at the doorstep, we hold it up high so the rain rolls right off, and we keep the pointy spokes away from everyone — big swings are for playgrounds, not pavements. When the rain stops, we fold it, strap it and let it dry by the door."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "An umbrella is a little rain roof you carry with you."
  2. Read the picture: the bus driver at a rainy bus stop opens his navy umbrella, holds it up high beside a small girl in a yellow raincoat with a pink backpack, keeps clear space around the open canopy, folds it with the strap, leans it by the bus door and checks a phone showing a rain cloud and 70%.
  3. Learn the parts together: canopy (the roof), spokes (the ribs underneath), runner (the slide that opens it), handle (where we hold). Open one slowly and count the spokes.
  4. Set the two rules as a pair: umbrellas open OUTDOORS, at our doorstep spot — and we keep them up high and away from eyes, including on the crowded pavement, where we hold them still and give everyone room.
  5. Practise the fold until it clicks: close, smooth the fabric, wrap the strap, stand it by the door to dry. Done well, it is deeply satisfying.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a bus driver in a navy cap, light-blue shirt and tie stands at a rainy bus stop with a blue bus behind: he opens a folded navy umbrella, holds a wide open umbrella up high beside a small child in a yellow raincoat with a pink backpack, holds the closed umbrella tilted down with clear space around it, fastens the strap on the folded canopy, leans the folded umbrella by the bus door, and points at a phone showing a rain-cloud icon and 70%.

Ask your child

"What are the parts of our umbrella?" "Where do umbrellas open — and where never?" "Why do we hold it up high?" "How do we carry it when the pavement gets busy?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Open at the doorstep, up high, away from eyes!" count the spokes proudly, or report the fold: "Strapped and drying — click!"

Out in the real world

Watch umbrella manners on a wet school run: who gives room, who pokes, who jabs through gate gaps — and be the family that does it right. Spot the big versions: market umbrellas, café parasols, the flat canopies over bus stops. Notice where wet umbrellas live indoors: stands, trays, hooks by every good door.

Try it together

Umbrella school on the doorstep: open, hold high, walk a line of teddies giving everyone room, fold, strap, stand to dry — full certification ceremony included. Canopy-count: how many spokes on ours? Then the rainy-day parade: favourite toys ride under the real umbrella on the wet pavement, perfectly dry and thoroughly delighted.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do umbrellas open? How do we carry them in a crowd? What happens when the rain stops?" Doorstep, up-high-and-away, fold-and-dry — your child now carries their own roof, courteously.

Parent tips

Give the rule a place, not just a no: "Umbrellas open at the doorstep" works because the doorstep is satisfying and legal. Choose a child umbrella with a blunt tip and a runner that needs a push-and-button (not a flick) — safer mechanics for keener hands.

Staying safe

Umbrella safety: open outdoors only, away from every eye; keep the pointy spokes still and spaced in crowds; never poke, jab or sword-fight; mind the runner so small fingers do not pinch; and on gusty days the umbrella stays home — wind flips canopies, and the raincoat wins those days.

This lesson pairs with the Umbrella flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Raincoat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes the raincoat routine automatic: what waterproof fabric does, the four moves — arms in, zip up, hood on, sleeves down — the hood practice that wins over hood-haters, and the hang-it-on-the-peg finish that keeps tomorrow’s coat dry.

What is this?

A raincoat is a coat made of waterproof fabric with a hood and a zip: rain lands on it, beads up and slides off, while the clothes underneath stay completely dry.

What does it mean?

The raincoat works as a system — the hood saves the head, the zip seals the front, the sleeves cover the wrists, the pockets flap over their openings. Miss one part and the rain finds it: the unzipped collar, the pushed-up sleeve, the bare head in a downpour.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three raincoat ideas: the raincoat keeps clothes dry so bodies stay warm; the sequence is arms in, zip to the top, hood up, sleeves down — all four, every rainy day; and after the rain, the coat hangs on its peg to dry, ready for next time.

Why this matters

The raincoat is the gateway garment of self-dressing: the zip is a milestone, the hood is an sensory hurdle, the sequence is memory work — and unlike the winter coat, it is light enough to practise daily. A child who owns the raincoat routine walks to preschool as the boss of their own dryness.

What it teaches

Four-step sequencing, zip fine-motor work, sensory tolerance (the hood!), responsibility for drying and stowing, and the pride loop of staying dry because of what I did myself.

Words to learn

raincoatwaterproofziphoodsleevespegdrydrizzle

Say this to your child

“"My raincoat keeps the rain off my clothes. Arms in, zip to my chin, hood over my head, sleeves down past my wrists — four moves and I am waterproof. After the rain, my coat hangs on its peg to dry, ready for the next grey morning."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The raincoat is your waterproof shell — rain knocks, but it cannot come in."
  2. Read the picture: the teacher with a bun and a green cardigan picks the yellow raincoat from a hanger on the coat rack, slips it on over her cardigan, zips it to the top, pulls the hood over her head, checks her sleeves are down, and hangs it back on the peg rack to dry by the door.
  3. Teach the sequence as four beats with actions: ARMS (both in), ZIP (bottom tooth to the top), HOOD (over the head), SLEEVES (pulled down past the wrists). Chant it on drizzly mornings until it runs itself.
  4. Practise the hood gently, never in a rush: hood-up in a mirror game, hood-up on teddy, hood-up for one slow count of three — tolerance grows in play, not in panic.
  5. End the ritual at the peg: after the rain, the coat hangs up, zipped open to air, hood flipped out. Tomorrow’s dry coat is tonight’s small job.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a teacher with dark hair in a bun, wearing a green cardigan over a white top: chooses the yellow raincoat from a hanger on a wooden rack with a blue and a pink coat behind, slips her arms in at the blue door, zips it up to the collar, pulls the hood on over her bun, checks the sleeves down to her wrists while standing by the open door in the rain, and hangs the coat on the peg rack to dry with her back to us.

Ask your child

"What are the four raincoat moves?" "Which part keeps the rain off your head?" "Why does the coat hang on the peg after rain?" "What happens if we forget the zip?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might chant it solo: "Arms, zip, hood, sleeves!" report from the mirror: "Hood up — I can still see!" or do the finish unprompted: coat on the peg, hood out, "Ready for next time."

Out in the real world

Spot the raincoat system at preschool pickup: every good coat rack has hooks at child height and space for wet coats to air. Watch the zip-workers at the door. Notice who is dry by lunchtime — the four-moves crowd — and who arrived soaked: the collar-open, hood-forgotten crowd. The sequence is the difference.

Try it together

Four-moves race on a dry day: arms-zip-hood-sleeves against the clock, then teaching the sequence to teddy. Hood-desensitising game: peek-a-boo hoods in the mirror, then hood-up for a slow three-count, then a hood-up dance move. Peg-practice: the hang-it-dry routine as a fine-motor challenge — coat on the hook, hood out, zip open to air. Certification: your child runs the door-check for the whole family on the next drizzle.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the four moves. Why the hood? What do we do with the coat after rain?" Arms-zip-hood-sleeves, head-dry, peg-to-dry — the routine now belongs to your child.

Parent tips

The hood is the hill to take slowly — never force it down in a hurry, because a hood fight at the door poisons the whole routine. Practise in play, choose coats with hoods your child likes, and accept hood-today-hair-tomorrow. And keep the peg low: the drying step sticks only when the hook is within reach.

Staying safe

Raincoat rules: all four moves before the door, in real rain — the damp-drizzle compromise is how colds catch rides. Check the zip does not catch chin skin, and the hood tie (if any) is not a long loose cord. Hang wet coats to dry properly: a damp coat tomorrow is a shivery child by lunchtime.

This lesson pairs with the Raincoat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Rain Boots — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes the boots routine child-owned from pull to peg: what waterproof boots do, the pull-on wiggle with the heel-all-the-way-down check, the sole inspection before the wet pavement, puddle judgement — splashers versus monsters — and the tray by the door that ends the wet-sock era.

What is this?

Rain boots are tall waterproof boots of rubber or plastic, worn over socks on wet days. They rise above the ankle so shallow water stays out, and their ridged soles grip wet, shiny ground.

What does it mean?

Boots change the maths of a rainy day: wet ground becomes walkable, puddles become toys instead of hazards, and feet stay warm because they stay dry. The tall shaft guards against the shallow slosh; the sole guards against the slip. Both deserve a quick check before the door.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three rain-boot ideas: boots go over socks — the wiggle test makes sure heels are down and toes can wiggle; soles get a quick check for grip and stones before wet ground; and puddles are judged — small splashers are for stepping in, deep monsters and kerb-side ones are for stepping around.

Why this matters

Boots are usually the first weather garment a child masters alone — which makes them the confidence engine of the whole wet-day routine. And puddle judgement is genuine risk assessment at child scale: which water, how deep, where does it lead? That thinking grows up into every safety decision after.

What it teaches

Independent dressing (the wiggle), observation and comparison (soles, puddle depth), risk judgement at a safe scale, responsibility for kit (tray, drying), and the pure gross-motor delight of sanctioned splashing.

Words to learn

rain bootswellieswaterproofwigglesolegrippuddlesplash

Say this to your child

“"Rain boots are waterproof feet for wet days. Socks on, toe in, push and wiggle — heel down, toes free. We check our soles for grip, we splash the small puddles, we step around the deep ones and never at the road. After, the boots live on their tray by the door, drying for tomorrow."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Rain boots are waterproof feet — wet ground cannot get us now."
  2. Read the picture: the crossing guard in a yellow high-visibility jacket chooses yellow boots from a shop shelf of colours, sits on a bench pulling them on, kneels to check a boot sole on the wet pavement, steps carefully around a puddle at the zebra crossing, gives a thumbs-up under her umbrella, and sets the boots on a black tray by the door at home.
  3. Master the wiggle: sit, point the toe, push, then wiggle — heel all the way down, toes free. Do the squat-check: a little jump — did the heel come up? Then down again and re-wiggle.
  4. Check the soles like the guard: flip one boot — is the grip pattern clear of stones? Slippery soles slip; grippy soles grip. Feel the difference on the doormat.
  5. Draw the puddle map after the next rain: splashers (green circles) and monsters (red Xs) on your street. Walk it together — child as the map-reader.

Look closer at the picture

The rain-boots card follows the crossing guard in her navy cap and bright yellow high-visibility jacket: she picks yellow rain boots from a shop shelf stacked with green, pink, purple and navy pairs, sits on a bench by a blue door pulling a yellow boot on, kneels on wet pavement pointing at a boot sole beside a pedestrian-crossing sign, steps carefully around a puddle while holding her stop sign, stands under a navy umbrella giving a thumbs-up in the rain, and places both boots on a black tray by a door where a pink coat hangs on a hook.

Ask your child

"What does the wiggle check?" "Why do we look at our soles?" "Which puddles may we splash?" "Where do the boots live after the rain?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might report: "Heel down, toes wiggling — good to go!" grade the street: "That is a splasher, that one is a MONSTER," or finish the routine: "Boots on the tray — dry for tomorrow."

Out in the real world

Visit a boot shop and let your child pick from two joyful options — ownership starts at the shelf. Check real soles after a wet week: worn grips versus new grips, felt on the doormat. Study the big puddles on your street after rain: where do they form, why there, and which are always monsters?

Try it together

Wiggle-school with a jump-check finish. Puddle-map cartography after the next rain — green circles and red Xs, laminated if possible, consulted proudly on every wet walk. Sole-compare: grippy versus smooth on the doormat. And the sanctioned splash finale: full kit, chosen splasher, one mighty two-footed jump — socks stay dry, and the child knows exactly why.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the wiggle do? Why check soles? Which puddles are never for splashing?" Heel-down, grip-and-stones, and kerb-side-never — waterproof feet, fully managed.

Parent tips

Boots over bare feet cause rubs — the sock rule is non-negotiable and worth saying once, clearly. Let the colour be loud: the child who adores their boots asks to go out in rain. And hold the line on monsters: the map works because the judgements are real, and real judgement needs a real no sometimes.

Staying safe

Boot safety: socks always under boots; heels all the way down or the trip risk doubles; soles checked for worn grip and lodged stones. Puddles: splashers yes, kerb-side and road-edge puddles never, and nothing deeper than the boot top — monsters are for looking, not wading.

This lesson pairs with the Rain Boots flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Sun Hat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns the sun hat from a wrestle into a routine: what the brim actually does, choosing the hat that the child will actually wear, the fit check — brim level, strap snug — and the hat-plus-shade-plus-water pairing that keeps summer play going strong.

What is this?

A sun hat is a hat with a wide brim all the way around — its job is to make shade: over the face, the ears, the neck. Many have a chin strap or cord so games and gusts cannot take it.

What does it mean?

The sun hat is wearable shade. Put it on and the head instantly sits in its own cool patch — you can feel the difference in one second. That felt feedback is the whole trick: the hat sells itself to the skin, if we let the child feel it work.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three sun-hat ideas: the brim makes shade for face, ears and neck; the fit check is brim level, strap snug — snug for safety, not tight; and the hat works as a team with shade breaks and the water bottle — the summer three.

Why this matters

Hat routines built on felt comfort and child choice survive every summer after — hat routines built on nagging dissolve by June. This lesson is as much about letting the child own the gear as it is about the gear itself, and ownership is the only sun protection that does not need reapplying.

What it teaches

Self-care routine ownership, fit-and-function reasoning (why the brim, why the strap), choice-making within limits, the felt science of shade versus sun, and the habit-stacking of hat-plus-bottle as one summer gesture.

Words to learn

sun hatbrimshadestrapfitcoolplaygroundbright

Say this to your child

“"My sun hat makes my own shade — brim over my face, strap under my chin, and my head stays cool even in the sun. Hat on before we go out, hat stays on while we play, water bottle close, and shade for our rests. That is how we do bright days."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The sun hat is shade you wear — your own travelling patch of cool."
  2. Read the picture: the playground supervisor in a yellow shirt chooses a blue sun hat from a shelf of yellow, pink, green and beige hats, puts it on by the playground, checks the fit with her hands at the brim and the chin strap, sits on a bench in the shade of a big blue sail, drinks from a blue water bottle and holds a thermometer reading 26°C.
  3. Do the felt test: ten seconds in the sun hatless — then hat on. "Cooler, right?" Let the skin argue for the hat.
  4. Learn the fit check as two hands: one levels the brim over the eyes, one snaps the strap — snug enough for a finger, no looser. Now jump: does it stay?
  5. Pair the routine: hat on, bottle filled — the summer three (hat, water, shade) as one door-chant before every bright outing.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a playground supervisor with dark curly hair in a yellow polo shirt and a name-tag lanyard: picks a blue sun hat from a wooden shelf of hats in yellow, pink, green and beige, places it on her head at the playground, checks the fit with both hands — one at the brim, one at the chin strap — sits on a bench under a big blue shade sail, drinks from a blue water bottle with one eye happily scrunched, and holds a white thermometer reading 26°C.

Ask your child

"What does the brim do?" "How do we check the fit?" "Who picks your hat — and where does it live?" "What two friends come with the hat on hot days?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "My hat makes shade — feel it, cool!" run the fit check aloud: "Brim level, strap snug," or chant the three at the door: "Hat, bottle, shade!"

Out in the real world

Visit the hat shelf together — two choices, child picks, done. Notice the shade-workers at the park: the sail over the sandpit, the canopy over the swings, every good bench angled to the trees. Watch who else wears brims: gardeners, builders, beach lifeguards, the whole outdoor-professional crowd. That is the hat’s reputation talking.

Try it together

Shade-mapping in the garden or park: where does the hat’s shadow fall — draw it in chalk. Hat parade: decorate the chosen hat with the child’s name or patches. The strap-jump test as a game. And the routine rehearsal: hat on, bottle filled, shade spot picked — then out, with the felt-cool check one more time so the skin signs off.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the brim make? How snug is the strap? What comes with the hat on hot days?" Shade, one-finger-snug, and water-and-shade — the hat is now a habit, not a fight.

Parent tips

Two hats double the odds: one by the door, one in the bag. Let the child pick the hat from a limited menu — a hat they chose is a hat they wear. And model it loudly: the grown-up hat goes on first, every time; the routine survives on visible grown-up compliance.

Staying safe

Sun-hat safety: brim level so it shades, not blocks, the view; strap snug but never a loose cord near climbing frames — check it against playground equipment; and the hat is one of the summer three: it works with water breaks and shade rests, not instead of them.

This lesson pairs with the Sun Hat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Sunglasses — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson completes the sun-safety set: what glare is and why eyes squint, the two-hands-on routine for real glasses, the mirror fit check, where glare is strongest — water, sand, snow — and the golden rule that stays true with or without glasses: never stare at the sun.

What is this?

Sunglasses are glasses with dark lenses that cut down bright light and glare. They come in every frame colour, in child sizes, and they live in a case or on a hook when the sun goes in.

What does it mean?

Bright light bounces — off water, sand, snow, pale pavements — and that bounced glare is what makes eyes squint and water. Sunglasses dim the glare so eyes stay comfortable. They are comfort gear for bright days, and they work as the third member of the sun team: hat, shade, glasses.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three sunglasses ideas: sunglasses dim glare so eyes stay comfy in bright light; the routine is two hands, gently on, comfy check in the mirror; and the golden rule never changes — sunglasses or not, we never look straight at the sun.

Why this matters

Sunglasses are a child’s first owned optical device — putting them on carefully, storing them safely, understanding what they do. The care routine (case, not pocket) and the honest physics (glare bounces) make this a small lesson with big cross-over: respect for tools, respect for eyes.

What it teaches

Two-handed fine-motor routine, tool care and storage, light-compare observation, the body-signal link (squinting means glare), and rule-keeping under temptation — the never-stare rule tested and held.

Words to learn

sunglassesglarebrightlensesdimfitcasesquint

Say this to your child

“"On very bright days we wear sunglasses — they turn the brightness down so our eyes stay comfy. Two hands, gently on, comfy check in the mirror. And the big rule never changes: we never look right at the sun, with or without glasses."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Sunglasses are dimmers for our eyes on very bright days."
  2. Read the picture: the pool instructor in a navy polo picks red sunglasses from a display rack of yellow, red, blue, purple and green pairs, puts them on with both hands, adjusts the arms over her ears for fit, stands looking toward a shaded canopy by the pool, wears them with a straw sun hat, and drinks from a clear water bottle with the pool bright behind her.
  3. Teach the routine as three moves: BOTH HANDS (one each side), GENTLY ON, COMFY CHECK (mirror, straight, no pinch). Practise until it is smooth and slow — glasses are handled, never grabbed.
  4. Do the light-compare: bright room, then sunglasses on — how did the light change? That dimming is the glasses doing their job for the eyes.
  5. Set the golden rule in stone: sunglasses dim the glare, but they are never a licence to stare — the sun is a no-look, always, with or without glasses.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a pool instructor with dark curly hair in a navy "pool instructor" polo and a whistle lanyard: chooses red sunglasses from a display rack holding yellow, red, blue, purple and green pairs, puts them on with both hands by the pool, adjusts the arms over her ears, stands in profile looking toward a blue shade canopy and bench, wears the red glasses under a straw sun hat while adjusting the brim, and drinks from a clear bottle with the sparkling pool and bunting behind her.

Ask your child

"What do sunglasses do for our eyes?" "Show me the two-hands routine." "Where does glare bounce the most?" "What is the golden rule about the sun?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Squinting means glare — glasses please!" run the routine solo: "Two hands, gently on, comfy check," or guard the rule: "Never stare — not even with glasses on!"

Out in the real world

Feel the glare by water, sand or fresh snow — bounce you can see. Spot who wears glasses for work: lifeguards, sailors, skiers, drivers — all glare-fighters. Let your child carry their own pair in its own case: tool care is the hidden curriculum of this lesson.

Try it together

Mirror-school for the two-hands routine until it is ballet. Light-compare lab: sunny window, glasses on-off — report the change. Glare hunt with hats on: which spot by the pond bounces hardest? Choose-your-pair from two options — then the care routine: case click, hook hang, never the pocket.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do sunglasses dim? What is the handling routine? Does the never-stare rule change with glasses on?" Glare, two-hands-gently, and never-never — eyes officially equipped.

Parent tips

Let some children opt out happily — the hat and the shade carry the load, and glasses are a bonus layer, not a battle. Pick real-dim lenses over toy dress-up sets if real wearing is the goal. And rehearse the never-stare rule out loud with the glasses ON: dark lenses can make staring feel safe when it is not, and saying so beats hoping.

Staying safe

Sunglasses safety: two hands, gentle handling — grabbed glasses break and broken bits are eye-hazards; real-dim lenses, not clear dress-up toys, if comfort is the goal; cases protect lenses and eyes alike; and the golden rule stands over every other line in this lesson — never look straight at the sun, with or without any glasses at all.

This lesson pairs with the Sunglasses flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Scarf and Gloves — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson adds the neck-and-finger team to the cold-day kit: why those bits chill first, the scarf wrap that is snug but never tight, gloves-versus-mittens by feel, the warm-finger check — and the tuck-it-in rule that keeps scarves safe on climbing frames.

What is this?

A scarf is a long soft strip of fabric wrapped around the neck to hold warmth in. Gloves give every finger its own cosy sleeve; mittens keep all the fingers together in one warm pouch.

What does it mean?

Necks and fingers are the body’s cold-out posts — thin skin, far from the warm middle, always exposed. That is why they feel the cold first and why the scarf-and-glove team matters: the scarf holds a pocket of warm air at the neck, and covered fingers keep their wiggle for playing.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three scarf-and-glove ideas: necks and fingers feel cold first, so they get dressed on purpose; the scarf wraps snug — never tight — with ends tucked in; and on playgrounds the rule is tucked or off, because loose ends can catch on slides and frames.

Why this matters

This lesson teaches precision care: warm is not just more layers, it is the right layers on the bits that need them. The wrap on teddy then on self builds the skill gently; the mittens-versus-gloves choice gives the child a real decision; and the tuck-in rule folds safety into the garment itself.

What it teaches

Fine-motor wrapping and tucking, body-map awareness (which bits chill first), choice-making (mittens or gloves today?), caring-for-others practice via teddy, and safety reasoning about loose ends and equipment.

Words to learn

scarfwrapsnugglovesmittensfingerstuckwarm

Say this to your child

“"On cold days our neck and fingers feel the cold first, so we wrap our scarf snug — around, then tuck the ends in — and pull on our gloves or mittens. Wiggle test! And when we play on the climbing frames: tucked or off, because loose ends catch."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Necks and fingers get cold first — so we dress them on purpose."
  2. Read the picture: the park ranger in a green hat and jacket picks a yellow scarf from a rack of purple, blue and red scarves, wraps it around her neck in the snowy park, pulls on a brown glove, wiggles both gloved hands warm, zips her jacket over the scarf and points at a forecast reading minus 4 degrees.
  3. Learn the wrap in two steps: around the neck, then tuck the ends in — snug enough to feel cosy, loose enough for one finger underneath. Practise on yourself, then on teddy (teddy sits very still and appreciates everything).
  4. Do the mitten-versus-glove try-on: which lets your fingers wiggle apart? Which feels warmer right now? Let your child choose by feel — both are right.
  5. Set the play rule like a rhyme: "Tucked or off for the slide and the climb" — loose, long ends stay home or get tucked before any playground gate.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a park ranger in a green wide-brim hat with a badge and a dark green jacket stands in a snowy national park with pines and a park sign: she picks a yellow scarf from a wooden rack of colourful scarves, wraps the yellow scarf snugly around her neck with both hands, pulls a brown glove onto one hand, holds up both brown gloves with fingers spread, fastens her jacket zipper over the scarf, and points at a tablet reading −4°C with cloud and snowflake icons.

Ask your child

"Which bits feel cold first — and why?" "Show me the snug wrap." "Mittens or gloves today — and how do they feel different?" "What is the playground rule for scarves?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might report: "Snug but one finger loose — perfect!" announce the choice: "Mittens today — warmest!" or recite the rhyme: "Tucked or off for the slide!"

Out in the real world

Watch the winter workers: every builder, ranger and dog walker has the neck-and-finger team on. Try the one-hand-in-cold-air test on the walk: gloved hand and bare hand, same wind — which taps the fence longer? Clip or string your child’s mittens to the sleeves and never chase a lost one again.

Try it together

Teddy-wrapping school: the wrap, the tuck, the praise. Mitten race: hands in, thumbs out, first up wins — then reversed with the non-favourite hand. Warm-finger science: bare-hand versus gloved-hand in the cold air, timed by who gives up first. And the rhyme-run at every playground gate: "Tucked or off!" before the first climb.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which bits chill first? How snug is the wrap? What happens to scarf ends at the playground?" Neck-and-fingers, one-finger-loose, and tucked-or-off — the team is now on duty.

Parent tips

Buy duplicates of the mitten your child loves — the lost-mitten tax is real and pre-paying it preserves peace. Let the choice live with the child (mittens or gloves, scarf colour, wrap style) inside the two rules: snug-not-tight, tucked-or-off. And wrap teddy first, always: the skill lands softer through paws.

Staying safe

Scarf and glove safety: snug, never tight — one finger must fit under the wrap; ends tucked in, and on slides or climbing frames the rule is tucked or off entirely; no long cords attaching mittens through coat hoods or car seats; and wet mittens get swapped for dry at the radiator, not endured.

This lesson pairs with the Scarf and Gloves flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Winter Coat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson crowns the winter kit with its boss level: how a padded coat actually works, the flip-over trick that ends doorway battles, zipping from the very bottom tooth, layering the hood and scarf like the card — and the car-seat rule every family needs before the first frosty drive.

What is this?

A winter coat is the warmest coat in the wardrobe: thick padding that traps a layer of warm air around the body, a cosy lining, deep pockets and usually a fur-trimmed hood for snowy gusts.

What does it mean?

The coat works by trapping: the padding holds a blanket of still, warm air close to the body, and the shell keeps wind out of it. Fastened properly — zipped from the bottom up — it keeps that blanket sealed. Over clothes it is the outer layer; under it, jumpers add more trapped-air blankets.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three winter-coat ideas: the coat holds our warmth like a sleeping bag we wear; the skills are the flip trick and the bottom-up zip — both learnable, both celebratory; and the car rule is big and non-negotiable: bulky coats come OFF in the car seat, with a blanket over the straps instead.

Why this matters

The winter coat is the Everest of self-dressing — big, stiff, long-zipped — which is exactly why mastering it matters so much. The flip trick gives a four-year-old a genuine technique, the solo zip gives genuine pride, and the car-seat rule gives the child words for a safety rule that even some grown-ups miss.

What it teaches

Big-garment motor planning (the flip!), multi-step zipping strength and control, layer-order reasoning (coat, then scarf, then gloves), safety rule ownership, and the confidence shift from dressed-by-someone to dressed-by-me.

Words to learn

winter coatpaddingzipflip trickhoodlayersfastencar seat

Say this to your child

“"My winter coat holds my warmth close like a walking sleeping bag. I flip it on — popcorn! — then zip it from the bottom tooth all the way up. Hood up if it snows, scarf in the middle for extra warmth. And in the car: big coat off, straps snug, blanket on top — that is how warm and safe ride together."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The winter coat is a sleeping bag you wear — it holds our warmth close."
  2. Read the picture: the bus driver at a snowy school-bus stop lifts the blue padded coat from its hanger, slips it on over her uniform, zips it to the top, pulls the fur-trimmed hood up, adds a red scarf as a warm middle layer, and holds up a white thermometer to check the cold.
  3. Learn the flip trick: coat on the floor, hood at your feet, arms into the holes, flip it up overhead — popcorn! The coat lands on your shoulders by itself. Practise until it is a party trick.
  4. Master the zip from the BOTTOM: bottom teeth together, slider down low, hold the bottom with one hand, zip up slow. The bottom-up habit is what makes long coats zippable at four.
  5. Teach the car rule with the coat itself: in the car seat, the big coat comes off — padding makes the straps sit too loose to hold us — arms out of the coat, into the seat, straps snug, then blanket OVER the straps. Practise it once in the garage so the real trips run smooth.

Look closer at the picture

The winter-coat card shows a bus driver in her navy uniform cap marked BUS, white shirt and tie, at a snowy stop before a yellow school bus and a blue bus-stop sign: she lifts the blue padded coat with its fur-trimmed hood from a hanger, slips it on over her uniform, fastens the zip to the collar, pulls the fur-trimmed hood up over the cap, wraps a red scarf around her neck as a middle layer, and holds a white thermometer to check how cold it is.

Ask your child

"Show me the flip trick — where does the hood start?" "Where does the zip begin — top or bottom?" "What goes over the coat for extra warmth?" "What happens to the big coat in the car seat?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might shout the move: "Popcorn!" mid-flip, narrate the zip: "Bottom tooth… slider… up we go!" or own the car rule: "Coat off, straps snug, blanket on top — I know why!"

Out in the real world

Watch the flip-trick crowd at preschool drop-off — the coat-flyers versus the arm-wrestlers. Check the coat before the season: zip glides? hood turns the head? cuffs still snug? Do a parked-car rehearsal of the coat-off-straps-snug-blanket-on routine once, calmly, before it matters in the morning rush.

Try it together

Popcorn-practice until it is show-off material — then the coat-flip demo for the whole family. Zip-ladder: from the bottom tooth, one tooth at a time, celebrating halfway and summiting. Kit-order line-up: coat, scarf, gloves laid out in wearing order by the child. Car-seat drill as a teddy lesson: teddy’s big coat off, straps snug, blanket over — "because padding hides the snug."

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me the flip trick. Where does the zip start? What is the car-seat coat rule?" Popcorn, bottom-tooth, and coat-off-blanket-over — the boss level is cleared, and the child knows it.

Parent tips

The flip trick is the single best gift in this lesson — ten patient minutes of practice buys years of doorway peace. If zipping stalls, share the job: grown-up starts the slider at the bottom, child runs it to the top; finishers come back tomorrow. And say the WHY of the car rule out loud once, clearly: padding hides how snug the straps really are — the blanket keeps the warmth without lying to the straps.

Staying safe

Winter-coat safety, in order: the car-seat rule comes first — bulky coats off in the seat, straps snug against clothes, blanket over the straps; zips checked for chin-catch and smooth glide; hoods down indoors where they block the view and snag on hooks; and a properly fastened coat beats an open one every frosty day — the trapped warm air only works when it is sealed.

This lesson pairs with the Winter Coat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).

Questions to ask along the way: Which tool would you want on the balcony? What does our thermometer at home say?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Rain goes in the gauge, wind moves the sock and the vane — the thermometer minds the heat.

Parent tips: A pinwheel or cheap windsock on the balcony makes this sheet come alive all week.

Understanding check: Hold up a finger as a thermometer: what does it measure? Then a finger windsock?

Real-life practice: Build the box invention for real from a cup and a straw, if the design bug bites.

WEATHER WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 34 · AGES 4–5

Weather Words Matching — solve it right on the sheet.

Match four weather words to their pictures, circle rainy-day clothes, sort hot from cold and trace the word SUNNY.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then match, circle, count, trace and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Every kind of sky has a word, and every word asks for its own clothes and things.

Knowledge to have ready: Sunny, rainy, cloudy and windy by picture, and which clothes answer a rainy day.

Why this activity matters: Word-and-picture matching is the strongest vocabulary glue there is — weather words are just the friendly subject.

  • Weather vocabulary
  • Clothing choices
  • Hot and cold sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Drawing the day

What to say before you start: Four skies, four words — let us wire them together so they never come apart.

What to look for on the sheet: For the t-shirt and shorts hiding in the clothes row — the rainy day does not want them.

Questions to ask along the way: What word is our sky today? What would you wear for it?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Rainy-day kit keeps you dry: start from the boots and build up.

Parent tips: Do the draw box standing at a real window — checking beats remembering.

Understanding check: Say one hot thing and one cold thing from the sheet, in one breath each.

Real-life practice: Tonight at dinner, name today's weather word and one thing you wore because of it.

WEATHER WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 34 · AGES 4–5

Wind Direction and Compass — solve it right on the sheet.

Follow the arrows to name wind directions, match north, south, east and west to the compass and catch the flag blowing left.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then match, circle, count, trace and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Wind has a direction, and direction has words — left, right, up and down first, then north, south, east and west.

Knowledge to have ready: The four arrow words and the four compass points on the rose.

Why this activity matters: Direction words do double duty — they read the wind today and maps tomorrow.

  • Direction words
  • Compass points
  • Observing flags
  • Word tracing
  • Left and right certainty

What to say before you start: Wind never sits still — but it always goes somewhere. Let us name where.

What to look for on the sheet: For the second flag: its tail points left, which means the wind is pushing left.

Questions to ask along the way: Which way is the washing-line flag pointing? Where does north sit in our bedroom?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Arrows wear their meaning on their tip — the pointy end tells the truth.

Parent tips: A phone compass turns the bedside into a treasure hunt: find north, then east.

Understanding check: Ask which hand is left — then which way the wind blew in section three.

Real-life practice: Watch a real flag or treetop on the walk home and call the direction together.

WEATHER WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 34 · AGES 4–5

Windy Weather — solve it right on the sheet.

Match the four weather words, circle what a windy day calls for, finish the sky pattern and trace the word WINDY.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then match, circle, count, trace and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Windy is the weather you can hear — and it brings its own things: kites up, hats held, umbrellas tucked.

Knowledge to have ready: Windy next to its three cousins sunny, rainy and cloudy, and the kite as the windy-day star.

Why this activity matters: A sky pattern that repeats teaches prediction: what comes next is thinking, not guessing.

  • Weather vocabulary
  • Windy-day choices
  • Pattern completion
  • Word tracing
  • Drawing movement

What to say before you start: You cannot see wind — only what it pushes. Let us spot the pushing day.

What to look for on the sheet: For the umbrella: it opens on rainy days, but wind turns it inside out — that is the thinking test.

Questions to ask along the way: What does wind do to your hair? What flies in wind that will not fly on a still day?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Say each word with its sound — whoosh for wind — and the matching gets easy.

Parent tips: Throw a paper aeroplane on a still day and a windy one, then report back to the sheet.

Understanding check: What comes after the second cloud in the pattern? Answer before pointing.

Real-life practice: On the next windy walk, name three things the wind is moving — bins, leaves, anything.
